speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The House had a wide-ranging discussion on climate issues, viable policy changes and proposals and the trade-offs for our economy and jobs, among other concerns.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Despite the enormous strain on our national resources to battle the COVID-19 pandemic, our Ministries and Government agencies have been pressing ahead to make the transition to a low-carbon society a reality.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And I wish to take this opportunity to express our appreciation to the Ministries and agencies for their hard work during this very difficult period.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened by my fellow Members' support for mitigation measures and their commitment to sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The green sector is developing rapidly in response to the climate emergency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, there are many new and exciting opportunities in the green economy, particularly in green financing and many new job roles in the sustainability sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, the GPC is also concerned about the lack of standardisation in accounting standards and the problem of greenwashing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, we are appealing for the firm hand of the Government to strengthen corporate accountability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And central to our transition to a green economy, our priority is to ensure Singaporeans are not left behind as the world progresses towards a sustainable future and economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to create fulfilling opportunities in a region with a growing sustainability sector and equip Singaporeans with the relevant skillsets and experience.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to help our businesses get ahead of the curve in sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For today's debate, I would like to share some general observations on Singapore's green efforts and my views on green jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My fellow colleagues in the Sustainability and Environment Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) will also share their concerns and recommendations in the three areas of green financing, green jobs and corporate accountability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Ms Hany Soh will join me in speaking about jobs in the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Gan Thiam Poh will share their views on green finance and carbon trading.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Ms Nadia Samdin will address the issues of green finance and challenges in Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) auditing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, several members of the GPC for Trade and Industry will also be joining this debate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They will share the green aspirations, as well as the concerns from the business community.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They will discuss how Singaporeans can seize opportunities in this new pillar of growth, the trade-offs between environment sustainability and economic sustainability, as well as the importance of upgrading skills and transforming jobs for inclusive transition to the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Environmental scientist, Nominated Member of Parliament Prof Koh Lian Pin will also be speaking about the importance of carbon offsets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Last Friday, the Young PAP (YP), published its second paper on climate change, entitled "Developing a Green Ecosystem".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many of us share deep concerns for our environment and for Singapore’s future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We hope to have the support of the whole House on this critical topic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Before we all dive into today's debate, let us recap some facts to better appreciate the scale of this climate crisis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us reflect and take stock of the measures that have already been implemented, to set the context for a productive discourse.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, it may appear that any impact from reducing our carbon emissions is correspondingly limited.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding, fighting climate change is a global effort and we should all continue to do our utmost to reduce our carbon footprint, as a nation, as organisations and as individuals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The question here is whether we can make a bigger impact in the global community.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can we contribute more to the global efforts to reduce carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And the answer lies in our role as an enabler, intermediary and facilitator.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We can build on our existing infrastructure as a global financial hub, to serve the region as a green finance hub and carbon trading centre.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a green finance hub, we will be able to bridge international capital with green solutions and innovations from different parts of the world, facilitating efforts to reduce carbon emissions far beyond our shores and in magnitudes way beyond our own.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is how we can punch above our weight and continue to contribute much more significantly to global carbon emissions reduction efforts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are also the world's fourth largest global exporter of high-tech goods, producing five of the world's top ten drugs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Despite our size, Singapore is actually one of the world's leading energy hub and chemicals hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To cut industry emissions, the Government and the private sector will need to work together to help industries transition into the green economy, with customised solutions to address specific industry needs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Green technology will be vital in the transition to manufacture more sustainable products that are also produced with better energy efficiency.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Green finance will be essential to fund these new technologies and businesses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With these new economic activities, there will be creation of new green jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, going green will impose additional costs to businesses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To sustain this green journey for the long haul, we need to strike a fine balance between environmental sustainability and economic sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Different types of businesses will need different timeframes to transit and transform.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some businesses will need more time to deal with stranded assets as a result of the green transition.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need viable and progressive transition timeframes for businesses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, if we set too onerous targets, certain industry players may actually relocate to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Instead of creating more green jobs in these businesses, we may inadvertently shift existing jobs along with their carbon emissions to somewhere else.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must also be mindful that for reasons of national strategic interests, we may need to continue certain critical activities which generate a substantial carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One example is desalination which is rather energy-intensive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, we may have to make some painful trade-offs and sacrifices in order to meet our national carbon emissions commitment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Thirdly, more than 95% of our power generation is from natural gas, which is still a form of fossil fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The reality is that Singapore faces severe constraints on the production of renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our wind speeds are not fast enough for wind turbines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We do not even have enough space to mount more solar panels.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, our neighbouring countries have abundant renewable energy resources.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government is already working to import renewable energy from Malaysia, Indonesia and, further afield, Australia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Indonesia, for example, will be a very valuable collaborative partner.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It has already committed to making sustainable development a key focus.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Presently, renewables still comprise a small part of its energy sources at 11% and there is much room for its geothermal, hydropower, solar, wind, biofuel and biogas energy supplies to grow.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It has set for itself the goal of almost doubling renewables in its energy composition to reach 23%.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Renewables now contribute 18% to Malaysia's energy mix, with hydropower accounting for 86% of its renewable capacity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Philippines has abundant clean and renewable energy sources, such as geothermal, hydro, wind and solar.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Its National Renewable Energy Program (NREP) 2020-2040 has set a target of 35% share of renewable energy in the power generation mix by 2030 and 50% share by 2040.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is much scope for our ASEAN neighbours to work together, pooling financing and engineering expertise to mitigate climate change.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With our complementary strengths, we can work together to achieve our carbon commitments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A few months ago, at the United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP26, consensus was finally reached on the set up of the international carbon market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The resolution of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement was critical.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Countries will be allowed to trade emissions reductions as well as assist other nations in reducing emissions without trading.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Private enterprises can invest in projects to sell green energy credits.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The resolution of Article 6 is extremely important to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will be a win-win strategy for alternative energy negative countries like Singapore and for developing countries requiring funds for renewable energy projects and for environment conservation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   At the recent United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP26, countries agreed that trading emissions reductions and providing assistance to other nations to reduce emissions, can count towards their carbon reduction pledges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This framework will provide us with valuable opportunities to collaborate with our neighbouring countries to work on emissions reduction and building infrastructure for renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In doing so, Singapore will be able to fulfil our climate change obligations and help this region reduce its carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For these projects, very importantly, we need Singaporeans with the specific deep cultural and linguistic understanding of our regional partners to ensure the success and longevity of our transnational collaborations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, our national representatives working at every segment and level – project management, engineering, human resources, legal, and more – need to have the language skills and contextual understanding of how things are done in our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many new jobs will be created, not just high-tech green jobs, but also green collar jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, there will be a strong demand for those who are willing to pick up the necessary skills for these positions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): I will now talk about green jobs and equipping Singaporeans to take advantage of opportunities in the sustainability sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As we make the transition to a low-carbon society, almost all sectors will be affected and new green jobs will be created in finance, trading, technology and innovation, legal, engineering, governance, education and more.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our education system will need to prepare and train Singaporeans and residents of all ages willing to learn in these areas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is challenging, in this fast-evolving landscape, to draw up new and updated syllabuses, recruit and prepare the trainers and roll out high quality courses in a timely manner to meet industry needs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Major updates and changes to course modules at our ITEs, Polytechnics, and Institutes of Higher Learning will be required.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Green activities and projects should be integrated into all disciplines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Institutions can consider integrating modules that expose and equip students from different disciplines with skills sets relevant in the sustainability sectors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Arrangements for internships and apprenticeships in these sectors will have to be made, and these would require the support of both MOE and MTI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The YP paper has proposed a Green Space Academy to groom local experts in research and development and technical experts, to sustain a pipeline of well-trained and specialised talents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the short- to medium-term, the fastest way to roll out the training courses is to piggyback on our current education institutions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Modular courses will allow students of all ages to enrol and accumulate credits towards certification.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is flexible and inclusive, especially for workers looking to switch to careers to join the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should consider borrowing from the German model, which is also being adopted by the Chinese government.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Young Germans split their time between classrooms at a vocational school and on-the-job training at a company as apprentices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The participation by German companies is high – about 80% of Germany’s large enterprises.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In October last year, China’s State Council issued a new guideline to have a similar arrangement to build a world-class vocational education system by 2035.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For Singapore, we can implement a similar system, by creating very tight and dynamic relationships between education and training institutions, research and industry stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should also watch out for the workers, especially the older workers, who risk unemployment if they are unable to adapt to new positions or pick up new skills during the green transition.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many green positions, even green collar ones, may require IT skills which may be more challenging for our senior workers with lower levels of education.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, I urge Enterprise Singapore and SkillsFuture Singapore to work closely with the labour unions to equip senior workers with relevant skill sets for the green jobs, so as to minimise job displacements as companies transit into the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Motion calls for an inclusive transition to a low-carbon society and this must naturally include our SMEs – the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government launched the Enterprise Sustainability Programme (ESP) to support Singapore businesses on sustainability initiatives, and to capture new opportunities in the green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My concern is whether this amount will be enough and whether our SMEs will be guided as to how to apply for and utilise this programme.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was announced that the support will come on three levels - developing enterprises' capabilities in sustainability, strengthening sector-specific capabilities, and fostering a vibrant and conducive sustainability ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many SMEs are struggling with day-to-day operations and trying to stay afloat.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How will they know how ESP will be relevant to them?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope more of such initiatives can be implemented.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to request that Government agencies be more open and allow SMEs to try out innovative solutions that can help reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such innovative and green solutions can help companies with a big fleet of motorbikes and self-employed delivery riders go green, without massive investments in motorbike charging infrastructure by the Government.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We ought to be responsive and learn from the best green practices in other cities similar to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: After all, acceptance of different ways to solving problems is necessary for innovation, which will drive our tech and development sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (in English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the transition to the Green Economy is like a fast-paced mass marathon.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On one hand, we are racing against time to mitigate this climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you recall, this was what I said one year ago, when this House came together to declare climate change a global emergency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, somehow, the world has become even hotter and even wetter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In China’s Henan province, a year’s worth of rain fell in a single day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And it is not just heat and rain either.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The science is clear: climate change will increasingly usher in extreme weather and throw lives and livelihoods into disarray.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As an open country, Singapore will undoubtedly be hit hard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a grim picture, and we are running out of time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is why my fellow GPC Members and I have returned to this House just one year later to call again for the Government to take further steps to tackle climate change, to sharply reduce Singapore’s carbon emissions and urgently move towards an inclusive low-carbon society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the climate crisis worsens, the people of Singapore have taken up the fight in their personal and professional lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I shared the stories of some of these inspiring individuals in this House last year, including Esther, Lastrina, Xiang Tian and Wei Shan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I shared how it really is not common to see a business leader advocate about climate change like she does and how despite all her time working with titans of the industry, her inspiration comes from youths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This past year, she attended COP26 in Glasgow as a private sector representative with our activists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At COP26, Esther proudly flew Singapore’s flag and spoke at the Built Environment Leaders Panel, a main stage event.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is not just at COP26 where Singapore’s activists and businesspeople stand together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Back home, Esther led CDL’s partnership with young activists from the Singapore Youth for Climate Action, or SYCA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together, CDL and SYCA launched a campaign called "Keep Calm and Love Our Planet".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Climate change can feel too big, too difficult a problem for the youths of the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The campaign aims to dispel the sense of paralysis and instead motivate youths to take action against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you have not spoken to Esther before, I strongly encourage you to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She is a breath of fresh air, overloaded with enthusiasm and passionate about working together with our youths to save this planet we call home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And this brings me to the young leaders at SYCA – Lastrina, Cheryl, and Swati, who Esther works closely with.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, I shared how Lastrina co-founded SYCA in 2015 to shine a light on what young people can do for the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this milestone, other leaders have stepped up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastrina has empowered and inspired many others and this movement has grown.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two of the leaders at SYCA are Cheryl and Swati.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Passionate about fighting climate change, they attended COP26 as youth representatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But their journey to COP26 was full of challenges, involving complicated logistics and fund-raising.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, their go-getter attitude exemplifies exactly what we want to see from our youths today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They shared with me that, to quote: "We are cautiously hopeful because we are see changing mindsets and positive actions all around us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have seen our peers push for change and encourage positive impact through conscious food choices, recycling and sustainable energy use.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are students, entrepreneurs, teachers, artists and individuals in various professions among us who work tirelessly to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They inspire us to keep going and empower other individuals who have this shared vision of this world." Last year, I also shared the story of Xiang Tian, a young man who leads LepakInSG, a youth initiative that circulates environmental events to motivate others to get involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One year on, Xiang Tian remains optimistic about what we can achieve through collective action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He told me: "One thing that makes me hopeful is the increasing number of people who are learning more about the climate crisis and other environmental issues and taking actions to push for change." In the past year, LepakInSG has been active on social media, explaining the important environmental impact studies and baseline studies we have done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, Xiang Tian is still doing this infamously in his slippers, although I am aware he is finally not wearing his slippers today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He sacrificed them to be able to enter Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Xiang Tian tells me that LepakInSG has exciting plans coming up to facilitate discussions between green groups in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also very fortunate that at the PAP Youth Wing, we also have young activists working tirelessly on climate change issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Wei-Shan is one such activist, leading a team of volunteers who are passionate about making a serious difference.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have been on many late-night calls with the YP team led by Wei-Shan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year I talked about the familiar sight of her two young children on our many Zoom calls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like my daughters, they remain a regular and welcomed presence on our calls over the past year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Welcomed in most cases, except when my daughter Katie appeared completely naked when I was on a Zoom call listening to the Prime Minister’s National Day Rally live.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was horrified and I sure hope that no one, including the Prime Minister, saw.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Along them are countless other activists and citizens who have fought so hard against climate change in their own ways.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their call for action is loud and clear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government should commit to achieving net zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have pushed for this many times in this House now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is based on science; global emissions must be net zero by 2050 if we want to have any hope of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This runs not just against what science say is needed, it runs against what many other countries are doing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Already, 136 countries have set concrete target years for carbon neutrality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It includes nearly every developed nation in the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, the US, Australia and Israel also committed to reach net zero by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Government may want to focus on actions, not targets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I do thank the Government for taking the right actions: releasing the Green Plan and for sharing how it will transform Jurong Island into a sustainable chemical and energy hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will be harder to get to net zero by 2050 if we are not actually intending for that to happen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, setting a target in line with scientific and international standards set a strong message to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would help the Government achieve what it says is needed: a whole-of-nation approach to climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last October, Minister Grace Fu said, “We will continually review and enhance our climate targets.” I thank the Government for its openness to revising its targets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the increasing severity of the climate crisis and the potential for sparking a whole-of-nation response, will the Government commit to reaching net zero emissions by 2050?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second proposal today is that we increase the carbon tax significantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no question that the carbon tax is the most powerful tool we have to slash emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Everything else – from green jobs to green financing that we are debating is important, very important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Finance Minister Lawrence Wong said last October that this is too low.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How high should it be to sufficiently slash emissions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One range from the High Commission on Carbon Prices, which is supported by the World Bank, proposed that US$50 to US$100 is needed by 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The IMF similarly recommends a rate of U$100 by 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even higher prices have been suggested by LSE’s Grantham Institute, which proposes US$145 and the OECD, which provides a central estimate of U$147 My ask is that we look at the studies that have been done by these institutions and the principles for how they arrived at these prices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can adopt the principles and approaches to derive a price that Singapore needs to reach net zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An increase in the carbon tax will also mean an increase in tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will use this to help subsidise decarbonisation projects in the private sectors as well as limit the impact on lower-income Singaporeans by issuing more U-Save rebates or vouchers under the Climate Friendly Households Programme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us make this transition an inclusive one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final ask is that we expand the coverage of the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This covers around 50 facilities that contribute about 80% of our total carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be aiming for a higher coverage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Government set a high threshold to limit compliance costs by smaller emitters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But smaller emitters, those emitting at least two kilotonnes of CO2equivalent, are already “reportable facilities” and have to pay the costs of monitoring and measuring their emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that any additional compliance costs would likely be minimal, it would make sense for the carbon tax to cover all reportable facilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would, after all, be in the spirit of a whole-of-nation fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Emitters, small and large, have a role to play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fight against climate change must involve decisive action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the matters of net zero targets and carbon taxes, we need to move much faster.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through that sharing, I learnt that many people did not know who on earth Captain Planet is and that I really am getting old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am glad many went to find out about Captain Planet and the important message of protecting our planet.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am also a council member of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA) on a pro bono basis.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Every region of the world has been hit by extreme weather events that are growing more frequent and more powerful.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our neighbouring countries have been impacted as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These occurrences are the result of climate change from cumulative human-induced factors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And some of these changes – like the continuing rise in sea levels – are irreversible.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Left unchecked, the interconnected crises of climate, pollution and biodiversity loss will rapidly erode the very foundations of our existence.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since human activities have resulted in these changes, human activities can also slow down, halt or even, if we may dare hope, recede them.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By reducing activities with heavy carbon emissions and through investments in green projects, we can strive to make changes for the better.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green financing is an important enabler to catalyse the evolvement of our region's green economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As one of the key financial centres in the world, Singapore has a strong responsibility to communities most vulnerable and existentially threatened by climate change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore can catalyse the flow of capital towards sustainable development in the region.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should continue to take the lead in mobilising climate finance from a wide variety of sources, instruments and channels, including instruments to unlock the huge potential of private finance through the targeted use of public climate finance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our financial services industry, which includes banks, insurers and asset management firms, can play a useful role in promoting sustainable and green finance in Asia, if not the world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green finance, as one of the key programmes of the Singapore Green Plan 2030, can boost sustainability efforts in Singapore companies and compel companies to consider green projects more seriously.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MAS adopts an active approach in promoting sustainable financing in our financial services sector, including engaging financial institutions to consider environmental, social and corporate governance (ESG) criteria in decision making processes, supporting the adoption of industry standards and guidelines, encouraging industry-led capacity-building efforts and developing the green bond market in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should also tap into the growing investor demand across the globe for green financing products and projects with clearly defined environmental benefits.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The framework should detail how the proceeds from the green bonds will finance expenditures to help tackle climate change, biodiversity loss and other environmental challenges, while creating green jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The sectors where we can make a difference include clean transportation, renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention and control, living and natural resources and climate change adaptation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government should also perform annual allocation reporting and periodic reporting of metrics on environmental impacts and social benefits and ensure transparency for retail and institutional investors and other interested stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is elevating the standards of emissions monitoring and reporting in Southeast Asia so as to help the large emitters in the region to curb their carbon footprint and increase their access to green financing schemes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore can take the lead to devise ASEAN’s version of the Action Plan on Financing Sustainable Growth and follow-up with a Strategy for Financing the Transition to a Sustainable Economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Other areas we should look into include an ASEAN taxonomy for environmentally sustainable economic activities, sustainability-related disclosures for issuers and for financial market participants, the ASIAN green bond standard and corporate sustainability reporting which may also include carbon tax accounting especially when carbon tax is likely to rise in the near future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To create a sustainable future for Singapore, we need all hands on deck.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Every sector, business and individual need to play their part.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In promoting the adoption of sustainable business practices and reporting, the trade associations and chambers, or TACs in short, can play a key role as enablers and strategic partners of the Government.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: TACs or professional bodies can partner the Government to support the sustainability agenda by providing resources to drive adoption of sustainability reporting and green finance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sustainability reporting is an emerging area, and companies will need references to guide them in their disclosures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the introduction of the Singapore Exchange Regulation’s roadmap for mandatory climate-related disclosures, ISCA is also developing a series of guides to share best practices and guidance publications on green and sustainable finance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These publications include a roadmap to guide professional accountants on obtaining green and sustainable finance for their organisations if they assess that such financing fits into their corporate business strategy, and a best practice guidance on how businesses can disclose their green finance policies and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With such assessment, this will allow companies to better approach banks for the financing of their sustainability projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It leads to a virtuous cycle of sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is just one example of how a TAC can contribute to the sustainability agenda.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the TACs to collaborate and work together to impact all sectors of society as we progress in the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To support Singapore's move towards a green economy, there is a need to equip the workforce with the skills and knowledge to participate in the sustainability sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Citing the accountancy profession as an example, being stewards of capital and corporate reporting, accountants play a crucial role in accelerating business practices in sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, increased participation by the accounting and business fraternities is key in Singapore’s bid to become a leading centre for green and sustainable finance in Asia and globally.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Climate-related risk management is also an important skill to possess.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Accountants must be equipped to prepare sustainability reporting as more stakeholders and investors adopt environmental, social and financial performance metrics.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, auditors need to get themselves ready to verify such information.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both accountants and auditors must step up to meet the market demands for sustainability reporting and the assurance of sustainability reporting.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Beyond collecting, analysing and reporting sustainability-related information, accountants and auditors can be strategic advisors to help embed sustainability into a company’s strategy, decision making and reporting processes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is therefore a need for accountancy professionals to upskill so that they can fully inhabit their role in driving sustainability and meeting the rising expectations of businesses, economies and societies in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To engage the accountancy professionals, this is where we can involve professional bodies like ISCA.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand ISCA has developed a sustainability reporting strategy which aims to raise the capabilities of the accountancy profession in driving sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As part of its sustainability reporting strategy, ISCA will focus its efforts on capabilities development and career opportunities for the accountancy profession in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will include sustainability reporting and external assurance on sustainability reporting.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will greatly enhance the career prospects of accountants and contribute to Singapore becoming a sustainability accounting hub in Asia.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Singapore Green Plan 2030 is expected to bring new career opportunities and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This has created vast job opportunities and new roles for Singaporeans, especially the accountancy and finance professionals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To encourage accountants and aspiring accountants to take up sustainability-related roles, there can be greater efforts to raise awareness of the diverse roles in this aspect and to brand sustainability jobs as attractive career choices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, ISCA also shared with me that they plan to profile their members who have taken on sustainability-related roles to showcase the emerging demand for such talents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They will also connect employers in need of sustainability-related talent with their members who wish to embark on this track.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I call upon all Singaporeans to work with us as we progress towards a greener, more sustainable future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   We do not want Singaporeans to be left behind as the world progresses towards a sustainable future and economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also realised that the Government needs to provide some help to local our businesses because this is a relatively new area, and the size of the start-up fund is not small.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We hope to create fulfilling opportunities for Singaporean of all backgrounds in this new sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans should be brave and stand at the forefront, seizing these opportunities presented to them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would also like to thank the activists from the Young PAP for their detailed and passionate proposal to mitigate climate change.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are all aligned in recognising the severity of the climate change threat that is upon us and are mindful of the urgency of actions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Doing nothing or status quo is not an option.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a responsible global citizen, we take our climate change commitments very seriously.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we also know that transiting to a low-carbon society is a mammoth undertaking, especially for a small, alternative energy-disadvantaged country with resource constraints like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we hope to get to the promised land in double-quick time, we have to also ensure that the stakeholders are all able to keep up with the pace, achieve the outcomes we set out to do and importantly, sustain high level of public support throughout this sustainability journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There will be pain-points and trade-offs that we will need to be addressed and for us as a nation to make, as a society as well and as individuals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The obvious immediate concern of many businesses is the transition cost towards more sustainable and low-carbon business practices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This takes place against the backdrop of other worrying global trends, such as supply chain disruptions, protectionism and slower global growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As businesses look to lower their carbon footprint to meet the demands of their customers, or business partners or even their bankers, they may also experience higher capital outlay and operating costs, such as the need for mandated sustainability reporting, the requirements to adopt of low-carbon technology, or the use of greener but potentially more expensive raw materials.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Domestically, the source of higher cost pressures could also come from Government regulations, such as energy efficiency requirements and the carbon tax as Singapore strives towards more sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Externally, as the world decarbonises, it can also lead to rising energy costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses now need to ready for the next round of carbon tax increases, with the likely announcement at next month's Budget Statement by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The higher near-term business costs may well be the necessary nudge needed for businesses to pivot, and when overcome, can enable these sustainable businesses to reap good returns and capture new and greater market share in the longer-term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, it is pivotal that we closely support our businesses as they overcome the initial steep challenges in their transition journey to low-carbon practices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore has no domestic hinterland and we compete with the rest of the world to sustain our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In some markets and industries, we may also face competitive comparisons as a place to invest and conduct business, with competing economies who have fewer sustainability requirements or are less strict in their implementation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The carbon tax is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We recognise that having carbon tax sends a clear signal that we are serious about decarbonising our industries and to become more energy efficient, and therefore spur the necessary industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But on the other hand, the impact to our businesses would be that companies may be disadvantaged when competing with jurisdictions that do not impose such taxes, or provide exemptions for some carbon-intensive export-oriented sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, some of these sectors in the EU, China and South Korea do receive free allowances under their emissions trading systems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And closer to home, in South East Asia, there are still economies who compete with us that levy no or lower carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The short-term impact on business competitiveness and compressed margins may be inevitable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses would need to rely on or strengthen their other competitive propositions such as quality and reliability to defend or grow their market share.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But, in the longer term, sustainable businesses may have a competitive advantage as consumers increasingly demand sustainable products and services.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we have to pace out the incremental increases so that our industries would not be dislocated and businesses can carry out the transition while staying as a going concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is also important for Government to be open about the timeline to increase the carbon tax so as to give businesses time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Inevitably, there will be businesses that may not be able to break even or cope with the carbon tax increases and may exit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to minimise such casualties and help as many businesses as possible to transit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While the healthy tension by way of carbon tax is necessary to nudge practices, it must be complemented by support measures from the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For SMEs, they can tap on the Enterprise Sustainability programme to build capabilities for the green transition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I urge the Government to continue reviewing these measures, taking in feedback from businesses and consumers, and enhancing the support where necessary.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is an emergence of green growth areas, such as in electric vehicles, green financing and research and development (R&D) of the low-carbon technologies and solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some of these areas are more developed, while others are more nascent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore needs to ride on this green wave to seize the economic opportunities and not be left out.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a country with limited resources, we need to identify the key strategic growth areas for Singapore that builds on existing strengths such as our position as a business and a financial hub.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also newer sectors that we can go into by leveraging our strengths in R&D.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, R&D presents a pathway for Singapore companies to develop new capabilities, technologies, and innovative products and services in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Such solutions are particularly sought after in carbon-intensive sectors such as power generation, industrial processes, transportation and construction.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To seize green growth opportunities, it is important for the Government to support and partner the industries and businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have done it before to grow globally competitive industries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should and can do it again to grow a thriving Green Economy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to develop the talent pool for Singapore to remain as an attractive destination for businesses, especially for those who place a premium on sustainability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can expect more jobs to be greener.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is therefore important for the Government and businesses to help workers to equip themselves to take on these green jobs, whether within existing sectors or in new sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Time and opportunity cost on the part of the workers must be factored in to allow them to acquire the new skills and adapt to a greener business environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are pain-points we will need to address to ensure a smooth transition for businesses and people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I agree that corporations have a crucial role to play in this transition and that the state and civil society, must be partners in the process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe, however, that the state must play a substantive leadership role and my remarks will address the various manner by which I believe it can do so as it guides the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, I declared that I am both a professor at a business school as well as the Chief Economist (Emeritus) of a wealth management advisory outfit, and occasionally speak on the topic of sustainable financing to audiences comprised of industry professionals and potential investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, even if one disagrees with the sweeping premises of either claims, it is probably fair to acknowledge that objectives that are subject to measurement, are more amenable to being targeted, whether in a practical or aspirational manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It makes inherent sense therefore for us to take more seriously the need to incorporate the core and the concept of natural capital into our national income accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Lest I be accused of introducing yet another annoying definition of capital to this House, I will start by emphasising that this concept is neither particularly novel – the term was introduced by German British statistician, E.F.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Simply put, natural capital refers to the stock of ecological assets such as fertile soil, forested land and coastal mangroves from which we receive essential services such as good harvests, clean air and water, and healthy fisheries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The term is now widely used across a number of disciplines, including anthropology, architecture, biology, geography, environmental science, economics, psychology and sociology; and the Prime Minister's Office – under the auspices of the National Research Foundation – has even supported an international collaborative project, entitled "Natural Capital Singapore".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the measurement of a concept that encompasses typically non-market ecosystem services, such as the richness of subsoil from which crops may be grown, the natural resources from which so much of modern communications technology is reliant on or the potential pharmaceutical innovations that could be discovered in a biodiverse forest, or even the cultural heritage that we receive from our understanding of our embeddedness in our terrestrial, coastal and marine ecosystems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this is challenging, such quantification is, in fact, not impossible, and the past decades have seen enormous advances in our ability to value natural capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2006, the World Bank launched the first of its reports aimed at measuring this natural wealth of nations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And just last year, the institution released its latest report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this should, perhaps, be unsurprising, given our surfeit of natural endowments, importantly, all of this accrues to renewable sources, which suggests that such capital can be protected, and perhaps even expanded, should we choose to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The vital need for us to preserve the little that remains of our forests, offshore fisheries, coastal mangroves, and protected land, rather than raze it all on the altar of urban development, is underscored by the recognition that we receive enormous benefits from natural capital, because properly accounting for natural capital alongside reproducible capital makes it clear that the former is a non-trivial contributor to the observed differences in the economic performance of rich relative to poor countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All nascent financial markets, and especially those in fixed income, benefit from the presence of a clear and trustworthy benchmark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This benchmark, more often than not, comes in the form of a government issuance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, it is worth thinking more carefully, therefore, about developing green financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the Government has been proactive in its efforts to encourage the development of green bonds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These initiatives are important, and I hope that the Government will continue to look for opportunities to further catalyse sustainable investment efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I am hopeful that all Government agencies will look for opportunities to weave in green financing elements into their capital expenditure projects and to fund these green components proportionately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure that administrators have strong incentives to conceptualise projects with sustainability considerations in mind – the stated goal of the 2030 Green Plan – since additional financing pools may, in fact, avail themselves when they do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, I hope that the public-private partnerships (PPP) in green bond issuance goes beyond the current co-investment in debt financing platforms to entail actual green development projects, especially in infrastructure, as well as equity contributions and loan guarantees issued by Government developmental financing vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is truly where, in my view, the strength of PPPs comes into play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I wonder if existing SINGA bonds will enfold green elements as well, and if so, whether this may mean a further expansion of the SINGA-related debt ceiling, and if there are plans for MAS’ Green Investments Programme to also include credit guarantees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, more fundamentally, we must not expect sustainable financing to be a silver bullet that will, in and of itself, be sufficient for our efforts to resolve climate change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our focus must remain on resolving environmental and climate change issues by dedicating real Government resources toward the emergency, rather than expecting financial markets to ride to the rescue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Through all this, we should avoid the temptation to satisfy ourselves with feel-good actions that amount to little, insofar as their genuine environmental impact is concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The current affinity, and some would call obsession, for environmental, social and governance – commonly referred to as ESG – investments is a case in point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most common refrain seen in marketing materials for ESG is that by investing according to such criteria, one could "do well while doing good".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This siren call is especially attractive to younger generations of investors, who both understand the critical import of long-term environmental sustainability, while simultaneously holding a deeply-felt desire to grow their money in a manner consistent with their conscience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet the promise of many ESG funds may well be a Chimera.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only do most ESG funds currently underperform a more mainstream index, many are expected to do so in future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Scepticism about the asset class is building, with at least one former ESG evangelist calling it a "dangerous placebo", while other observers fear that climate finance is now a financial bubble.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more critically, the underperformance of ESG relative to non-ESG investments is precisely the point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The converse of lower expected returns to green corporations is that brown corporations face higher costs of capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when capital is more expensive, these firms are likely to grow slower and, by extension, pollute less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the corporate front, we should likewise guard against claims by firms that proclaim environmental objectives but are only doing so for the veneer of sustainability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is impossible to perfectly police these so-called "greenwashing" attempts, Government should not be complicit in lending a stamp of approval to firms that are simply pronouncing adherence to such standards for the purposes of going through the motions or, worse, marketing reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As an example, consider one of the more egregious examples of greenwashing, involving carbon offsets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2019, a ProPublica report examined the market for carbon offset credit – the idea this House will recall – that firms would purchase carbon sinks such as trees to counter the pollution they would be creating – and concluded that most programmes, while not always blatantly fraudulent in that they would actually set aside forest land, nevertheless contravened the ultimate purpose of the scheme, since a large majority of projects involved forests that were either already protected or would never have been cleared anyhow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The report concludes that, and I quote, our "hunger for these offsets is blinding us to the mounting pile of evidence that they haven't – and won't – deliver the climate benefit they promise" and that "carbon credits for forest preservation may be worse than nothing." As an example, consider our current, single-stream recycling programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this approach surely encourages many to adopt a recycling habit, reports suggest that awareness of our recycling best practices remain low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The routine disposal of non-recyclable materials in our blue bins – such as styrofoam or plastic bags – is, I am certain, commonly observed by Members of this House during their estate walks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Further downstream, the practice of exporting recyclable waste runs the risk – as demonstrated by the Chinese treatment of most imported recyclables – of simply being redirected to foreign landfills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a third example, consider the booming market for sustainability bonds worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The result is a loss of credibility and efficacy that could undermine the entire purpose of the exercise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, corporations are primarily in the business of making profit, and market their goods and services in a way that enhances said profit as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But just as Government plays a role in regulating false claims of efficacy in pharmaceutical products or imposes conditions to ensure product safety in food and children’s toys, it should also play a role in ensuring that claims on green practices are broadly justifiable, rather than claiming caveat emptor and placing the entire burden of verification on the shoulders of the busy and often underinformed consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, Government can operate in closer collaboration with non-profit efforts – such as the Green Label scheme under the National Environmental Council – to ensure that such labels do not become an unwitting tool of unscrupulous greenwashing attempts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is worth exploring if such regulatory moves are warranted here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would have the added benefit of creating green jobs for our next-generation economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Having said my piece, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have all heard this phrase about the importance of finance – money makes the world go round.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Chinese has an even more imaginative phrase: 钱能使鬼推磨.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Meaning that with the right amount of money, one can even get ghosts to work for you.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the climate change crisis, we need to use all the tools at our disposal and, perhaps, the most powerful tool is the financial tool.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Appropriately structured financing can direct resources and efforts towards green projects and endeavours to mitigate climate change.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an international financial hub, Singapore will play a crucial role in ensuring financial flows from the public, private and not-for-profit sectors to our sustainable development priorities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Five months later, the Green Finance Industry Taskforce (GFIT) was set up to accelerate green finance by improving disclosures and fostering green solutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Corporates listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) are already required to disclose their environmental information through sustainability reporting, although as Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) and the Centre for Governance and Sustainability (CGS) noted, there is "ample room for improvement in the quality and depth of disclosures on quantifiable sustainability targets".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, such disclosures should not be marketing-style narratives of their green philosophy and policy statements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Outcomes and evidence of Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) impact, in addition to financial performance, consistency between policies and practices and supported analyses of asset-specific ESG risks should be quantifiable, verifiable and clearly presented in plain English.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All companies, not all listed ones, should have ownership of environmental management in their businesses and integrate sustainability into their business models.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider standardised green certification for all companies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The public will be able to view which product or service providers are awarded Green Certificates.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will be helpful information for consumers and motivate other companies to reach their desired green labels or targets.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Eventually, more and more enterprises will make sustainability an integral part of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government more organisational guidance and other forms of support to transition to green businesses, with courses for their staff to enrol in and linking them to relevant course enrolment websites, funding schemes and programmes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be good to have a standardised nationwide ESG Rating Index and methodology for companies' green evaluation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Financial institutions (FIs) can integrate sustainability into their business by making financing dependent on the implementation of social and environmental sustainability guidelines.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that the banks will take economic, social and environmental issues equally into account.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should avoid financing projects that are harmful for the climate on the one hand and invest in climate change mitigation and adaptation on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government can consider providing green finance participants with more incentives, such as tax exemption for qualified green deposits, bonds and funds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As green finance becomes increasingly mainstream, there will be a growing demand for retail products, such as green mortgages.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Improved consumer awareness will give individuals greater agency in choosing these financial products.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help stimulate demand for sustainable products.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Ministry can also establish national or industry awards for corporate sustainability evaluations to provide awareness and recognition for green companies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope more investment be made into technology with the use of the carbon tax to reduce, eliminate, capture and convert the carbon emission to improve the environment for us and the world and such technology shall be shared with all businesses, big and small, that produces carbon and operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The businesses shall be encouraged to continually look into sustainable and substantive solutions to the carbon elimination or conversion from bad to good and be rewarded for their effort and positive outcome.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government is still studying the use of high-quality international carbon offsets but to me, it is more important to reduce the emissions in the first place.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry can look into a system limiting the amount of offsets and providing incentives for the affected companies to adopt green transition processes and technology where available.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It could not have been timelier was we have seen more effects of climate change materialised over the last year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At home, intense rainfall events in 2021 led to heavy flash floods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the region, the floods in Malaysia and Typhoon Rai have led to hardship and suffering to the affected communities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The events remind us that climate change is at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This year, in this Motion "Towards a Low-carbon Society", Members of Parliament on the other side of the aisle is calling on the Government to advance Singapore's inclusive transition towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This builds upon last year's Motion as there were measures discussed, such as enhancing green financing, creating green jobs and strengthening corporate accountability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We, the Workers' Party, do not object to these measures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our inclusive transition also need to be just to address the unequal impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To put this simply, it aims to address inequalities, such that no Singaporeans will be left behind and all can aim for a better future in the transition towards the green economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Lest some in this House think a just transition is mere window dressing and holds no direct relevance to us, this very term can be found in the preamble of the 2015 Paris Agreement, of which we are a party to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The relevant paragraph notes, and I quote, "Taking into account the imperatives of a just transition of the workforce and the creation of decent work and quality jobs in accordance with nationally defined development priorities." If nothing else, our manpower and development policy should adhere to the spirit of the Paris Agreement by trying to stay in line with its goal of keeping global warming or limiting temperature rises to 1.5 degrees Celsius as we reaffirm by COP26 in Glasgow, last November.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This means that we need to ensure that green financing is not just catered towards greening the sources of energy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It needs to create value for our labour force.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We need to ensure that we can prepare those working in our high carbon intensive industries, particularly those in the the fossil fuel related sectors for new green jobs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We need to ensure that corporate accountability is not just about reporting their greening efforts, but how they are ensuring their own green transition includes bringing the many workers within and not lead to mass retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A just transition also means that green finance should not solely be about capturing profitable opportunities in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It should also be offering those that are left behind by a green transition, the funding opportunities to adapt.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They should concern those whose existing jobs and livelihoods are affected by transition, away from polluting industries, as well as those at risk of the direct impacts of climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How do we achieve a just transition for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This must be done in both words and deeds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Here, I have a few suggestions for the Government to consider.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And a commitment to this will give impetus to focus societal efforts on combating the global emergency, that is, climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This pledge also looks at supply chain development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore, as a shipping and logistics hub and a commercial centre, can and should play an important part in the global supply chain screen. transition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The average Singaporean worker must not only hear that we are doing the right thing but also sees the concrete benefits from this move towards a low-carbon sustainable economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should prioritise a roadmap for carbon intensive industries, such as petrochemicals and power generation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can also look at ensuring a just transition for the labour force.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For secondary industry, they are carbon intensive but are already taking active and laudable steps to adopt less polluting technologies, such as transport, shipping, logistics in the supply chain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should also consider a just transition roadmap to get our financial professionals to take on nascent green financing roles where there are growing opportunities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a just transition roadmap must be a key complement to the Singapore Green Plan 2030 on the green economy and be executed upon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will ensure that value is not just accrued within businesses only but an equitable share of the value created will directly benefit Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can also kickstart stronger efforts on green upskilling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the vein of ensuring our talent pipeline remains robust, I also ask that all our agencies ensure their future upskilling programmes and career conversion programmes are created for and geared towards the green economy we aspire to, so that the value of the green economy can be directly captured by Singaporeans, both present and future.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We, in this House, have seen robust exchanges on Motions surrounding climate change and jobs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have the opportunity here to hit two birds with one stone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us not waste it and seek a just transition for all Singaporeans workers in the greater future we seek to achieve.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The impact of climate change and the opportunities presented for a green and sustainable economy have never been more urgent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst sustainability efforts amongst companies in Singapore have gathered pace, the lack of understanding of sustainability and related concepts has been a barrier to galvanising strong action.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: During the recent Ecosperity Week held in September last year, it was revealed that some 250 chief executives of firms who have made net-zero commitments are unsure of how to reach their goals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From inconclusive measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) standards to a lack of agreement in defining sustainability performance, business leaders urgently need a framework to navigate their firms through these challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There remain many companies, especially our SMEs, who have yet to come on the green economy bandwagon.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They lack the understanding of its impact on their business and how to make the green transition; yet this is one of the most significant business opportunities that they can tap for business growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
