text: Certain industries may need additional support to spur decarbonisation ahead of others, in anticipation of carbon border taxes such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism which puts carbon prices on imports into EU.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given SMEs’ critical role in supply chains, we can boost their transition on three fronts: first, we can promote sector-based sustainability road maps with industry-aligned principles, frameworks and uniform standards; second, we need to support SMEs with pre-identified sector-based green solutions to fast-track adoption; third, we can leverage the ecosystem to build scalable green capabilities and collaborations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Speaker, a carbon tax assigns costs to planet-warming emissions and forces companies to consider the cost of pollution and environmental harm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Finance Minister Lawrence Wong has indicated that Singapore’s carbon price is too low and will be up for review.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is about 20 times our current rate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst the plan to increase carbon tax is imminent, we need to carefully calibrate the increase and consider the trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Too low, we fall short of our commitments in making a viable impact to nudge firms in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Too high, we risk firms passing on cost increases to consumers and end users, or worse still, moving business activities to countries with lower sustainability requirements and carbon pricing.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While these firms need to pay their fair share, there are some who are already pivoting their business activities towards low-carbon solutions in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, in 2020, Shell Singapore announced a 10-year plan to cut down local emissions by a third by the next decade.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Similarly, ExxonMobil collaborated with local Universities in launching the Singapore Energy Centre, forming centres of excellence in research and innovation to solve technological gaps amongst industry players.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is opportunity to work closely with such firms to co-create a sustainable future, helping transition high emitters of yesterday into green industry leaders of tomorrow, here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst Singapore’s headline amount of S$5 per tonne of emissions is low – it is low – but it covers 80% of local emissions with no offset provision.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In Southeast Asia, Indonesia is the only country other than Singapore which has announced concrete plans to introduce a carbon tax, at a minimum rate of US$2 per tonne of emissions only from 2022.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Trade-exposed sectors in the EU, China and South Korea receive free allowances under their emissions trading systems.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Speaker, Sir, whilst reviewing Singapore's model, we should note that there are more than 60 different carbon pricing initiatives worldwide.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Each regime adapts to different strategies based on its own goals and constraints.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst Singapore can learn valuable lessons from other jurisdictions, we need to develop our own unique playbook for carbon pricing and ensure any change is set and paced carefully to avoid dislocating our industries or losing our attractiveness as an investment location.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For instance, the Singapore Business Federation expects that carbon tax increases will impact the manufacturing sector hard, as utilities can comprise up to 9% to 10% of operating cost.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the rising cost of labour, freight and raw materials, any further increase in operating cost in the near term will adversely impact many companies already struggling in the current economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Currently, Singapore’s carbon tax does not apply to imports.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This puts local SMEs in a disadvantaged position as Singapore embraces more advanced integration of sustainable practices at increased costs, affecting these companies' cost competitiveness relative to peers in the region.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Many businesses have shown increasing interest in improving their environmental, social and governance performance.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, they want to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in their value chain, to meet carbon neutral or net-zero emission goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: However, many businesses are also finding it difficult and challenging to completely transition away from fossil fuels by mid-century.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Sunny Verghese, the CEO of Olam, made a telling remark during Temasek’s Ecosperity Week in October last year.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: After speaking to over 200 fellow chief executives who have made net-zero commitments, Mr Verghese realised that most of them may not know how to get there.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: So, while it is important to set ambitious targets for a low-carbon society, it may be even more important to develop and execute the strategies, policies and actions for us to achieve these goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: That is what this Motion is calling for and why I fully support it.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This will include putting an appropriate price on carbon to internalise the social, economic, environmental and climate costs of carbon emissions, as my fellow Members have highlighted.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: In a nutshell, it is a way for companies or individuals to invest in value-adding environmental projects to balance out their own carbon footprint.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Carbon offsetting as a concept may present various technological, political and ethical conundrums.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But insofar as decarbonisation remains the top priority and effective guardrails for carbon offsetting are in place, certain types of carbon offsets are not only viable, but may be indispensable, for us to meet our climate goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: A carbon offset credit is a tradable certificate or permit that represents the allowance to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide, or equivalent greenhouse gas.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: These carbon credits can be produced from different types of clean technology projects, emissions reduction projects or carbon capture projects, including both technology-based and nature-based solutions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Nature-based carbon projects are important because they represent low-hanging fruits for us to immediately turn off one tap of our carbon emissions by ending deforestation and start to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through reforestation.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Nature-based carbon projects, such as mangrove conservation and restoration, can also deliver many other benefits for local communities and biodiversity that are well-aligned with the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: But by the same token, we have the good fortune of being geographically situated in a region with bountiful opportunities to work with nature in our fight against climate change.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we have the ability and responsibility to work across sectors, nations and generations, to realise these opportunities and to help us transition to a low-carbon society.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps a more pertinent issue is to ensure that carbon offsetting will actually deliver the benefits it promises.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there are concerns about the lack of transparency in the global carbon marketplace today, in terms of the quality and pricing of carbon credits.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: This has posed a deterrent to both buyers and producers, and created a bottleneck to both the demand and supply of nature-based carbon credits.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, we need to ensure that carbon offsets are not being used for greenwashing to create a veneer of sustainability, as fellow Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim pointed out.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: There is always the risk that some companies or individuals might buy up carbon credits for environmental claims, without actually making any effort to reduce their carbon footprint.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we need to hold to high standards of accountability, both the buyers and producers of carbon credits.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: On the supply side, we need to ensure that carbon projects deliver real, additional and permanent benefits, not just for climate change mitigation, but also for communities and biodiversity on the ground.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: On the demand side, we need to ensure that users of carbon credits have in place, concrete policies, plans and actions to transition to a lower carbon economy, and are not relying solely on offsetting to reduce their net carbon emissions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The EST convened several Alliances for Action (AfA), which represent a new form of private-public partnership with a strong bias towards action in capturing new opportunities.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: And capture new opportunities the EST did indeed.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Who would have thought that one day, Singapore’s most important financial institutions – the engines of our economy – will play such an important role in the conservation and restoration of our natural environment?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: So, we are capable of thinking beyond the dichotomy of economic development versus environmental protection.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, a Clean and Green Global City has always been a national focus since our founding as a nation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We have been doing our part such as setting up a Climate Action Package in 2018 and more recently, putting forward the Singapore Green Plan 2030 which we discussed in this House.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In joining the debate on this Motion, there are two key areas I would like to touch on: one, factors to consider in our Green transition plans; and two, seizing opportunities in the Green economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These are areas that will pave a clear glide path in our journey towards achieving our net-zero ambitions and eventually set a time-bound commitment, along with strengthening our position on climate leadership.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Key to an effective green transition is about having a good implementation plan.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This requires a clear-headed recognition that a greener world and Singapore will come at a cost.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It was apparent at COP26 that such trade-offs are not easy to make and Singapore will face similar challenges in our transition journey.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A good implementation is about our Government leading these efforts which are effective in reducing real carbon footprint and done smoothly, so that the unintended effects on our society are mitigated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A holistic plan would entail: one, a balanced approach in carbon pricing; two, eliminating the regressive effects; and three, accelerating efforts on identifying enablers, which is about stepping up awareness and education on carbon emissions and greener alternatives.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we transition towards a green economy, the immediate concern of many households and businesses is about having to bear higher costs to adopt more sustainable and low-carbon practices.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will be taking place against the backdrop of other forms of global trends that is driving cost increases, such as supply chain disruptions, a topic we debated passionately about.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As businesses look to lower their carbon footprint to meet expectations of stakeholders, they will experience higher operating costs and capital outlay.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Domestically, higher costs can also arise from changes in regulations, such as energy efficiency requirements and the Carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Externally, as the world decarbonises, energy costs will rise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given this, the implication is not to stop or slow down our decarbonisation efforts but to ensure that we provide support to households and businesses in their journey to become more sustainable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is to allow households and businesses in particular SMEs, to make rational transitions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Higher businesses costs could be temporary during transition and eventually make our businesses fitter in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But transitions do take time, and our Government could consider adding "carrots" as part of a total package over and above the tax regime, such as Green rewards or financing incentives for households and businesses to accelerate behavioural changes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore’s transition plan towards a low-carbon society should be an inclusive one.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If we are to achieve a greener way of life, it is important to scale up awareness and educational programmes for households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This enabler is key to move from rhetoric of mere targets to real actions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many initiatives we do today, such as our Smart Nation or Zero-Waste Nation programmes, fits nicely into our green movement.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Such programs reinforce our green efforts, such as accelerating digitalisation, will lead to a paperless society and reduced waste will help go towards reducing carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: There is scope to create more awareness on enablers as well as actionable steps to galvanise actions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the global urgency to act quickly for a net zero carbon future, Singapore can and should seize the exciting opportunities that exist before us.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We can improve the lives of our citizens and contribute to the global good along with creating new business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As an international services hub for finance, consulting, accounting, trading and legal amongst others, we are well-positioned to help the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will also create many exciting green business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is often said in business, what you want to manage, you first need to measure.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While this is a critical step, the task of any company to determine its baseline carbon footprint or emission is not easy, even for a sophisticated corporate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol requires the measurement of not just this but also the indirect emissions from a company’s activities known as Scope 2 and from the value chain known as Scope 3, which is even more complex to measure.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What I am saying is that measurement is not easy and companies here and the region will need expertise to get this done.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Financial services is also an area where Singapore can make an impact.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This demand will spur the supply and diversity of products in the international financial marketplace, such as sustainability linked loans, green bonds, green investment funds, as well as transition financing to support decarbonisation plans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Another key opportunity will be for Singapore to position itself as a carbon services hub.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Today the carbon markets globally remain illiquid and fragmented as they face challenges such as the lack of strong governance, differing standards and grey areas such as the verifiability of projects.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Market participants wonder if the carbon credits purchased really deliver carbon reductions.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, the opportunities before us are real given the pent-up demand.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this is where Singapore can play a distinctive leadership role as a trusted global financial and services hub with strong regulatory regime, market infrastructure and services sector expertise.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our brand name for excellence will provide us the platform to create a carbon services hub where participants can buy and sell carbon credits that are of integrity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This would mean the need for an ecosystem such as carbon accounting and Monitoring, Reporting and Verification Services (MRV) here and in the region.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, there will be a need for more professionals in a carbon services hub ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will spur our services sector to leverage existing skillsets in areas such as trading, product structuring, measurement and certification to apply in the carbon space to support clients in their decarbonisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: All these will lead to the creation of new jobs in Singapore and in the region.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We can achieve this by implementing measures in a balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Transitions will require sacrifices and trade-offs by individuals and businesses, but the positive impacts created and the opportunities that can be seized will be bountiful.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, the future is an exciting one as there are many green growth opportunities for Singapore to scale while at the same time riding this wave to drive economic growth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If our generation does not set in motion sufficient changes to mitigate climate change, our grandchildren will pay a painful price for our lack of resolve and action.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will be infinitely harder for successive generations to reverse the impact of global warming, even if they try their best to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore incumbent upon our nation and the world to rise to meet this challenge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has in the past approached climate action as a small nation which is unable to make much impact on the vast world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This approach has thankfully evolved in recent years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, a greater resolve in our outlook towards this challenge is needed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We are still constantly reminding ourselves that we are a small country with inherent limitations as to what we can do to reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We wave the flag that our alternative energy disadvantage status is officially recognised by the United Nations' Framework Convention on Climate Change.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Certainly, these are realities that we cannot run away from.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we must not, in our attempts to temper expectations, allow these mantras to limit our imagination and innovation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, carbon dioxide does not respect national boundaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Arguably, the biggest impact that Singapore can have on averting climate change, and hence saving ourselves from the harm that global warming will do to us, will come from test bedding and developing new green technologies and sharing these discoveries with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Making low-carbon technology widely available at a reasonable cost will be critical to spurring industry adoption and helping the world to achieve net zero carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We may be small, but that does not prevent us from working around our constraints of a small land area, high urban density, hot tropical weather to innovate solutions that could mitigate climate change in an increasingly urbanised world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our constraints can actually be our comparative advantage over other nations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our green inventions could spread far and wide beyond our shores to benefit the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should therefore aim to make a global impact in our climate change efforts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should be prepared to make big investments in emerging green technologies and in doing so, take decisive steps towards wielding the mantle of climate leadership.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I wish to focus on a few of these green technologies and how the Government can play a bigger part to drive their adoption.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the transport sector, which is one of the biggest emitters of greenhouse gases in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Almost all the current plans for the rollout of EVs focus on battery electric vehicles (BEVs).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it may be risky to place all our bets on BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For starters, it is still unclear whether we will have the infrastructure to handle an all-BEV fleet of vehicles once ICE vehicles are fully phased out.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will equip only about 6% of public carpark lots and 3% of private carpark lots with charging stations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given that it takes anywhere from 30 minutes to six hours to recharge a car, and assuming people charge their cars only once every five days, my calculations indicate that the infrastructure will support only about 30% of cars in HDB estates and 15% of cars in private estates each night.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am, in fact, making optimistic assumptions about driver behaviour.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In reality, range anxiety will dictate that drivers will avoid waiting for their batteries to run flat before recharging them, just like we do not wait for our mobile phones to go flat before plugging them in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To avoid hogging the charging stations, one driver will have to hurry down to the carpark at 12.00 midnight to unplug her car and find another parking spot, while another will need to come down at the same time and plug his car into that same charging station.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Imagine the disruption to everyone's sleep rest cycle and the number of neighbour disputes that this would spark.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One possible solution to this problem would be for charging stations to serve multiple car lots at once, with an automated system that recharges the cars on a rotational basis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will spare drivers the need to unplug and re-park at night.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The technology for this already exists, but it is unclear if these types of chargers will be deployed in Singapore car parks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The batteries in BEVs are heavily dependent on two metals: lithium and cobalt.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to a study by Deloitte, BEVs account for about 27% of global lithium demand, while lithium-ion batteries account for about 59% of cobalt demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More than half of the world's cobalt comes from mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo and there are ongoing concerns about the health, human rights and geopolitical risks of mining this mineral.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Any disruption in supply of materials for BEVs might affect their production and raise their prices in future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Economists have warned against the possibility of "green-flation" caused by supply chain shortages, leading to higher prices for metals and minerals that are essential to EVs and other renewable technologies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have to keep this in mind that the mining of lithium and cobalt and the manufacture of lithium-ion batteries also produce large amounts of greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could negate some of the green benefits across the full cycle of BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A large number of BEVs will also place a heavy load on the electricity grid.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the grid be strong enough to support so many vehicles being charged at the same time, including many using fast chargers, which will drastically increase peak power demand?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The cost and carbon output of grid upgrades will need to be considered if you want to fully electrify our transport using BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) are another major type of EVs which are much less discussed than BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They run on hydrogen, the most abundant gas in the universe.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are more energy efficient than ICE vehicles and produce no harmful tailpipe emissions, only water vapour and warm air.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are powered by electricity generated by fuel cells through an electrochemical reaction between the hydrogen fuel and the oxygen in the air, facilitated by a fuel cell catalyst.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some might have safety concerns about the FCEVs becoming Hindenbergs on wheels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In terms of vehicle fires, leaks and explosions, FCEVs are measurably safer than ICE vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Hydrogen is much lighter than petrol vapours and dissipates much faster if there is a leak, reducing the potential for explosions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In any case, safety regulations will dictate that hydrogen fuel stations must store gas above the ground in well-ventilated areas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: FCEVs bring with them some advantages over BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, they can be refuelled much faster that BEVs are recharged.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Each BEV will require at least 90 minutes to fully charged using a fast charger and up to six hours using other types of chargers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, FCEV buses can refuel their hydrogen tanks in as fast as 10 minutes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, with improvements in technology for the production and distribution of hydrogen, FCEVs could eventually have a lower carbon footprint than ICE vehicles and possibly even BEVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the cost of production and distribution of hydrogen is much higher than diesel or petrol.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, many countries are devoting significant efforts to developing sustainable hydrogen production technologies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the benefits that FCEVs bring and some of the risks and disadvantages of BEVs, it would be prudent for Singapore to include FCEVs in our local mix of EVs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What are the steps that the Government is taking to transition our public transport and goods transport systems to use green hydrogen?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Hydrogen is not just useful as a source of clean energy for vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It also has multiple other industrial applications, including in clean power generation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: About 30 other countries, including New Zealand, the Netherlands, Belgium and South Korea, have already rolled out hydrogen roadmaps.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This national renewable hydrogen strategy will spur the creation of a hydrogen economy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should map out our plans to invest in the development of hydrogen technologies, propose new legislation, set national targets for low-carbon hydrogen and develop a pipeline of local talent to take advantage of careers in this emerging sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will set Singapore on a path towards being a global player in the hydrogen industry and benefit Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, even if this target is met, solar energy will still supply only about 4% of our total electricity demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given that solar energy is one of Singapore's most promising renewable energy sources, we have to make a much bigger push to develop it and set bolder targets for solar energy in our electricity mix.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Rooftops present one of the most promising platforms to deploy solar photovoltaic (PV) systems, given are highly urbanised landscape.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government's SolarNova programme is looking to install solar PV systems on the rooftops of public sector buildings, including HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I asked the Minister for National Development on 10 January whether HDB intends to install solar PV panels on all HDB block rooftops where feasible.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to note the Minister has replied in the affirmative.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should make a stronger push to install solar panels on all rooftops, both public and private, that do not have physical encumbrances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is similar to a call made by my hon friend, Mr Leon Perera back in 2017.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would greatly increase our solar energy capture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, EMA allows consumers to be paid for channelling the excess solar electricity back to the grid and BCA has a green mark scheme for solar panel adopters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, from a reply by the Minister for Trade and Industry to the Member of Sengkang Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, I note that the Government does not provide grants or subsidies to further incentivise the adoption of solar energy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This rings especially true in view of the current high electricity prices caused by supply, shortages of natural gas, which we are currently over depended on for power generation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a subject which I elaborate during the debate, on the Energy Resilience Bill last November.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should rethink its current approach and provide more incentives for solar adoption in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Landed properties, condominiums and commercial buildings provide a significant amount of rooftop space for solar panel deployment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the end of the day, this will still be a win-win for property owners and the nation, In conclusion, Mr Speaker, Singapore needs to be bolder and braver in setting green goals to secure our future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of these may be stretched goals today but we have to trust that future generations will discover breakthrough technologies to overcome our disadvantages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Technology is improving all the time and more so when huge resources of governance are being poured into research and development into low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to ride the technology wave; not fall behind it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If we take a wait-and-see approach to hydrogen and other technologies, we might start seeing even our neighbours overtake us.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will move the needle significantly to advance Singapore's transition towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During last year's Motion to accelerate efforts to address climate change and its impact on Singapore, I spoke about the importance of involving our community in our efforts to greenify the environment, raising greater awareness and encouraging more to shift towards an eco-friendly lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since then, the community has made good progress in embracing green living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The AGT initiative affirms the importance of combating climate change in creating a better home for every Singaporean, aiming to do so by achieving zero waste, energy-efficient and greener towns by 2025.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The actions in support of this mission are coordinated across the 15 Town Councils by an AGT taskforce and are driven within each PAP Town Council by a dedicated Sustainability Committee consisting of residents, Young PAP activists and an elected Member of Parliament responsible for championing sustainability efforts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The AGT taskforce is headed by Chairperson, Dr Wan Rizal and I am humbled to be appointed as the Sustainability Champion for Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC as well as the Vice-Chairperson of the AGT taskforce.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As incentive, residents can earn cash each time they drop in their waste paper to such machines for recycling.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have shared with this House before that in Woodgrove division, we have a "G.E.L" mission, where "G" pertains to "Green-Living" initiatives.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition to the efforts which were rolled out through the AGT taskforce, over the past one year, we have also conducted two sustainability dialogue sessions and organised 10 upcycling-related workshops and activities which have been participated by over 700 residents across all ages, all of these were made possible through collaborations and supports by our grassroots leaders and community partners, such as Tzu Chi Foundation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through these initiatives, we hope to grow more interest in our Woodgrove residents to embrace a greener living lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of my residents, Ernest Yen, is one of the active participants of our Sustainability dialogue sessions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a Year 1 Mass Communication student in Ngee Ann Polytechnic, he recently approached me to conduct an interview for his school project, during which he shared with me that he has decided to focus on "Green Sustainability Efforts in the Community" as the theme of his project, as he wishes to pick up new skills and play a part in the community effort towards going green.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moving forward in Woodgrove division, we intend to continue inculcating more youths like Ernest to become our green champions, through gamification along with increasing community engagements geared towards working adults and seniors, including those with mobility issues or other special needs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example would be our plan to collaborate with Northwest CDC to conduct a series of SkillsFuture workshops on sustainability to enhance green knowledge among the residents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These workshops will encourage residents to identify their interests, upgrade their skills and thereby create opportunities for them to explore green career options.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The increased exposure will hopefully lead to more supply of green talents to support sustainability in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some green jobs which will potentially be in great demand in the near future include built environment designers and engineers, sustainability consultants and green finance and investment managers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The built environment provides many opportunities for a career in sustainability, as each phase of a building or facility's life cycle, from development feasibility studies, design and construction, to maintenance, operations and demolition stages can be improved with sustainable strategies.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Education and upskilling via SkillsFuture courses will also be helpful in transforming many of these existing jobs in the built environment, with an added focus on being green and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the Edusave Bursary Awards last year, I had the chance to interact with many of our youths who have completed their "O" levels and are now pursuing a Diploma in the Polytechnics.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of the courses they are in fascinate me, one of them being the Diploma in Sustainable Built Environment offered by Republic Polytechnic, which aims to prepare students to take up roles as Energy and Sustainability Consultants.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like Li San, I believe we can develop more essential knowledge and skills modules focusing on sustainability in our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and accredited SkillsFuture courses, such as the Specialist Diploma in Environment and Water Technology, being a one-year course offered by Temasek Polytechnic, so that Singaporeans, both young and old, can increase their employability with regard to green industries.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, we can also provide more internship opportunities for IHL students to learn sustainability practices in various industries.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Aside from helping our workforce to learn the relevant skills for green jobs, we should also empower and encourage more Singaporeans to pursue their dreams and become green entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: John Cheng, Chairman of Feed9B, has shared with me that he hopes to build a food ecosystem that will not only provide a platform for collaboration but also to act as a resource and research centre ultimately championing Singapore's "30 by 30" goal and position Singapore as a global leader in food sustainability and innovation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This initiative involved agencies from various Ministries, including MTI's Pro-Enterprise Panel (PEP), Enterprise Singapore (ESG) and Singapore Food Agency (SFA).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: John is also the founder of Innovate 360, Singapore’s first food accelerator with shared facilities that assists startups in scaling and going to market.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They provide co-working spaces, test kitchens, shared laboratories and manufacturing facilities as well as opportunities for mentorship, funding, networking, distribution and collaboration with other firms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example of a recent collaboration was An Artisan’s Christmas SG Bazaar which showcased more than 30 Singapore brands that place an emphasis on sustainable materials and processes, innovative designs or a key part of our local heritage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was where I became acquainted with C2+, a local disinfectant manufacturer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These companies see themselves as a meaningful part of our nation’s journey towards reaching the goals set in our Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I do not think they deserve to be unjustly criticised by skeptics as “merely going through the green motion for publicity sake to generate profit” without first understanding how much effort these companies have actually put in towards steering their R&D and business operations towards being eco-friendly and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Last year, the Government announced the Singapore Green Plan 2030, setting out clear goals for urban afforestation, sustainable living and a green economy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, many businesses and jobs in Singapore can be transformed with green knowledge and skills through education and upskilling, aspiring to leave no one behind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Concurrently, this, in turn will contribute towards making our Singapore a greener and more sustainable living environment for all in the long run.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It rightly points out that in order to do so, there is much more to be done through the partnerships we built between the business, Government and people sectors in order to move Singapore's transition towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many advanced economies, like Japan, are setting bold targets of being carbon-neutral or even carbon-negative.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is, no doubt, even more important because of the pressing climate and resource crisis faced by everyone on Earth.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we, in Singapore, must do our fair share to bring about a green and sustainable future for our planet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party supports this and I would like to note now that, while important, moving towards being low-carbon and going green is only part of the wider picture of how our economy and society should look like in the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Changes need to be systemic and sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And being sustainable goes beyond just the environmental impact.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also includes the sustainability of the social, economic and cultural impacts that our industries and businesses have on our communities and these aspects are intertwined with and often inseparable from environmental matters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, while it is the case that we must urgently take bold and swift action to move towards a low-carbon society, it will be a massive missed opportunity if we deal with these issues in silos and our efforts to reduce our carbon emissions are taken in isolation from the social, economic and cultural aspects of sustainability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To achieve these aims, our businesses could take inspiration anew from John Elkington's original idea about the 3Ps – people, planet, profit – which he has since adapted to refer to people, planet and prosperity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, he has called for our industries to look to minimise negative impacts and to maximise our positive impacts on all three aspects.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I believe that there is much wisdom in this approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore, our businesses and industries are irreversibly plugged into the global trade and supply chain ecosystem.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even trends of glocalisation, exacerbated by the shocks brought about by the pandemic, have not reduced the complexity of our global supply chains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our position at the crossroads of many networks, whether they relate to physical trade, such as our importance as a trading port, or services, such as data centres, financial and fintech systems, means that we continue to be in a position to exert influence far beyond our shores.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We, therefore, must build credible, accountable and sustainable ecosystems for our businesses to thrive in beyond our borders where necessary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also be aware of cheap marketing gimmicks which serve the purpose of winning short-term customer favour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we should work together with our industries to rewrite the playbook to create genuine sustainable change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A few years ago, I was fortunate enough to, as part of my job, we are going to campaign within what was seen as a sunset industry to lead the charge to drive consumer and industry change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We created a campaign backed by the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals to set out clear direct steps for consumers and industry players alike to advocate in order to banish antiquated and unsustainable practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While tackling planet, the environmental and ecological impact of operations, we quickly realised that we also needed to address the people and prosperity elements in tandem to effect meaningful change for the industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This was no less because ensuring that smallholders were able to earn a living wage, in turn, reduced the likelihood that they would, as a matter of necessity, sacrifice long-term goals for short-term gains, which were often environmentally harmful in order to feed their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We thus worked with global and local NGOs to develop best practices and educational materials for workers to understand what they needed to do in order to keep safe while minimising the impact that they had on the environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These practices would maximise the long-term sustainability of the land and their livelihoods by adopting new technologies, such as adopting better ways of ensuring robust traceability in the supply chain for customers, be it B2B or end-users.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Education also had to be done to explain why the current pricing mechanism was lacking and also why they should demand sustainability when making their consumption choices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While working on agricultural sustainability practices in rural settings may seem a long way from best practices in our local urban context, the principle of ensuring genuine sustainability and environmental practices applies equally to us, as well as in our cross-border investments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is despite marketing messages on its website that promised customers that they will know that the chocolate has been produced in a way that supports the most vulnerable people and environments in the supply chain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While environmental and social issues as a corporation become increasingly critical, the Government plays a key role in holding corporations accountable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These examples illustrate the importance of a holistic approach to ensuring our planet and people continue to thrive and how we need to build the right corporate culture in Singapore across these various spheres of sustainability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also insufficient to allow companies to be mindful only of direct actions performed within our shores when they have wide impact abroad.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As mentioned, the intricate and complicated nature of the global supply chain makes traceability and accountability even more important than ever.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only then can we be certain that corporations and the products we buy and also what our Government buys, not only do not harm the environment and have minimal footprint but also do not participate in the exploitation of vulnerable peoples.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not always straightforward for companies to audit the practices of their suppliers or even going further upstream to ensure compliance up and down the entire supply chain, but we must not let perfection be the enemy of the good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Working with the Government to make best efforts to build more robust measures to place greater accountability across the system will make significant headway towards guarding against Singapore consumers being unknowingly complicit in some of the ails we read about, such as poor labour practices or the disregard of the environmental impact of practices up and down the entire supply chain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With this in mind, I have three suggestions to set us on this path.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This required companies to proactively build a view of the risks within their supply chain and to put in place procedures to mitigate these risks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This allowed companies to better evaluate potential partners and subsidiaries and also requires mechanisms to be put in place for workers and organisations to flag violations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach is especially relevant in the post-pandemic era where businesses everywhere are re-examining the sustainability of their supply chains and looking into whether they can be rationalised or even shortened.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is thus a perfect opportunity to weave in such considerations as part of the economy-wide rethinking.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of viewing this just as a cost, we can recognise the competitive advantage this could bring us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Whether or not strong incentives rather than legislation would be sufficient to encourage enough adoption of this, remains to be seen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, we must play our part on the global stage to strengthen the global regime for regulation around supply chains and to be an active player to support wider adoption of such practices internationally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure that the majority of competitors on the global stage invest in similar practices and will also ensure a level playing field.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it may take a while to get there, we should take heart from the recent adoption of the global minimum tax rate of 15% by 136 countries.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I know that, with the right effort, it can be done.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For manufacturing companies, introducing technology from the Internet of Things allows managers to seamlessly monitor performance of their production lines in real time and also enables accurate information about matrices, such as energy consumption and the carbon footprint of their processes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Blockchain technology tools should be looked into for traceability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It might seem gimmicky to see lobsters in the jumbo seafood tanks wearing tags with QR codes that tell you exactly where they were caught and by which fishermen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It allows the capture of information to allow for more efficient fleet planning and can raise an alert if overfishing is occurring.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also plays a role in consumer education, providing information such as the carbon footprint of their food and gives confidence that the food is traceable to its source and the technology is there to track and ensure that good sustainable practices are adhered to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These issues and ambitions may sound remote, especially in a world where many are struggling to put food on the table.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the reality is that we are facing a resource-scarce future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the long run, our local businesses would benefit from being encouraged to start building a sensitivity towards supply chain vigilance and can use this to set themselves apart from our competitors, especially in Asia, to lead the way in markets that put a premium on goods and services that are accountable and sustainable, this will give a big leg-up in the internationalisation efforts of these companies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That said, I want to bring this spotlight back to the importance of citizen awareness and activism, to amplify the effectiveness of any Government regulation or policy in this space.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When consumers are more aware and demand sustainable and green practices and have a mindfulness over the carbon footprint, the greater the incentive will be on companies to be aware of the risks within their supply chain and to adopt greener practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To be blunt, if investing in greener practices has no impact on how consumers buy, companies may then shrug and continue the business as usual.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To address this, we can take a few steps.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our students should leave the educations system with a solid foundation in the importance of sustainability and also with a vernacular to understand and analyse the information that they receive in the media and from other companies of the efforts that have been undertaken.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This vaccination against greenwashing, a topic which has raised by some of my colleagues, would enable consumers to be critical recipients and build a disincentive towards any greenwashing efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can identify blind spots and encourage innovative solutions and approaches that businesses may not have thought of.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to leverage the passion that these activists have to nudge our industries to do better.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These citizens will be inoculated against marketing gimmicks by both industries and governments that might disingenuously suggest sustainability conscious practices and instead generate an imperative on them to be truthful and transparent with citizens.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For after all, our society and economy would be nothing in a world facing climate meltdown brought about by shortsighted, unsustainable practices that fail to account for people, planet and prosperity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Spurred by pledges at COP26, we look to the future growth of green finance with cautious optimism.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, climate finance, green bonds and loans are firmly on the agenda of governments and central banks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the financial industry, increasing scrutiny and sectoral demand for ESG financing are pushing banks to green portfolios.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Greening will eventually take place across all industries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our green financing capabilities and frameworks need to be robust and ready to support these transitions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore’s financial landscape is notably shifting in tandem with these winds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both the private and public sector have rolled out laudable initiatives to support this transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is encouraging that we see more initiatives to enhance our green financing capacity, with the MAS acknowledging it as a powerful enabler to achieve an effective yet inclusive transition to net zero in the region.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the transition to a greener financing ecosystem is a challenging and complex one.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some businesses and operations might be ill-equipped to ride on and benefit from these winds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The central focus of my speech today is to highlight more ways we can support local businesses and the local ecosystem in green financing and accountability.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, there is a myriad of attempts to develop universal green loan and green bond standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Global funds that are linked to ESG-related standards more than doubled in 2020, compared to 2019.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More than ever, we need quality frameworks and regulatory support to empower financial institutions and businesses with the know-how of going green.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On an international level, the Green Loan Principles developed by the International Capital Market Association provides a framework for green financing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Regionally, we also see how ASEAN is participating in this effort with the ASEAN Green Bond Standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to more details on the training workshops and resources which will be available.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While opportunities exist, what is the take-up rate and how can we best support our local businesses, especially SMEs, in understanding and seizing them?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One possibility is encouraging financial institutions to increase the accessibility of green loans, especially for smaller firms, while providing the capacity building to do so.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some corporates have been trailblazers in the past few years, publishing green bond frameworks and corporate governance strategies at a company level for going green.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But it would be better if we also make it accessible for small players to participate in this process to ensure that compliance costs do not bog them down.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some specific measures could include greater clarity on what are green and sustainability-linked loans especially for SMEs, its benefits, criteria for businesses to access them and what exactly about their businesses and supply chains would need to change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most importantly, it should be clear to our businesses what specific impact-metrics need to be tracked, and how they can track them, perhaps leveraging on technology where possible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Businesses are empowered to assess their own eligibility for these loans when they have access to information and such tools.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And second, it provides greater transparency and accountability, to manage greenwashing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is in our interest to make green financing more accessible for all players, to allow as many actors as possible to participate and transform.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, we should try to acknowledge businesses for transitioning to more sustainable business models.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The catalogue could formally recognise businesses that undertook or are undertaking significant and genuine sustainability efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would increase their visibility and encourage consumers to support them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Entities interested in procuring goods and services from sustainable sources could refer to such catalogue.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Including specific measures which businesses have undertaken to go green in the catalogue would also be helpful to other local businesses who are interested in pivoting to more sustainable endeavours, as they would have a better understanding of best practices and how they can participate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, it would do well for us to have a national sustainability accounting strategy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given Singapore’s status as a financial hub, and increasingly, a green financing hub, we should continue to finetune our green financing and sustainable accounting standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore has stringent financial auditing frameworks, sustainability accounting is still a fairly nascent concept worldwide, and there is a high reliance on accuracy, transparency and reliability of disclosures that form the basis of such sustainability assessments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is greater recognition among stakeholders that ESG disclosures are necessary and not just a good to have.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When shifting winds are difficult to navigate, businesses are increasingly choosing to have third party auditors or second opinions to verify ESG disclosures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, such ESG assurance frameworks tend to be decentralised and varied.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The variety of frameworks could potentially create an obstacle to the consistency of the reporting, and comparison, of ESG performance across entities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The International Financial Reporting Standards Foundation announced the creation of the International Sustainability Standards Board during COP26.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is imperative that Singapore stands in lockstep with international standards for sustainability reporting.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that more guidelines and resources can be given to the relevant institutions and partners to understand and reconcile the myriad of reporting and assurance frameworks currently available.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, I hope that there will be further guidelines developed that are ASEAN-centric and Singapore-centric, to better cater to our local SMEs and smaller companies own auditing standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With stronger support and partnerships, the quality of our chartered accountants and auditing companies will remain first class as we further develop the sustainable accounting ecosystem at home.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we want to achieve regulatory clarity, it may be difficult to do when the green financing and sustainably accounting sectors are still rather new and it is unclear what the best standards are.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this challenge comes with an opportunity to position Singapore as a global leader in the green regulatory space, while enhancing our status as a green financial hub.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that regulations are complex and still emerging, there is room for policy and regulatory research to harmonise and raise the standards of sustainability.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has a golden opportunity to become a regional and even global thought leader in these spaces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The demand for sustainability auditing and green financing will certainly increase in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only can we ride on the winds of sustainability, but we can also redirect it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To become a leader in this space is not only for our own position as a nation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All countries will in time transition to green energy, transport and manufacturing systems, yet green technology, infrastructure and finance are not equitably distributed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the region, Singapore can play a critical role in the sharing of knowledge and collation of best practices, so that as a region we can tap on the opportunities in the green transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would spearhead regular sustainability-related MICE events to shape industrial innovation, attracting regional and international experts in the process.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would aid in attracting established global partners and budding brands in ASEAN to further the sustainability agenda.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Motion seeks good, inclusive environmental and economic outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I thank the young PAP for their continued dedication to the cause and publishing the Climate Action Strategy Position Paper.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: New methods of financing would, indeed, invite exciting opportunities for our businesses to grow and contribute to a greener economy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would like to reiterate that the greening process is not just about swapping out for new systems.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Businesses and consumers must realise and be prepared that this is ultimately a transition and it would also involve the process of unlearning, and shifting away from old operations, financing and activities that are unsustainable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is why we must continue to be bold, demonstrate our national commitment to support businesses and our people in the green and blue economies and to hold ourselves to high standards, so that together, our collective actions are impact-oriented.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our systems have started shifting in recent years to embrace these changes, but other than ensuring that systems are strong, they must also be accessible to our local businesses and people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Systems change works alongside individual action and there are many in the private sector and civil society who are tackling climate change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Underscoring the transitions in our systems is the opportunity for our people from all walks of life to be front and centre in this green economy, including taking advantage of the new jobs and career options.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us keep up the momentum and take concerted, sustainable action, as we build capabilities to transform and quite literally, try to save the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These are terms that are frequently associated with efforts to fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Before I share the reasons for optimism, let us do a quick stock-take of where the world is, after COP26 and after two years of pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We all read the disappointing recent headlines on coal power plants that were not categorially phased out, or how there was a lack of new ambitious commitments and how a lone US senator torpedoed America’s ambitions to go even greener.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But beneath these headlines is a tsunami of real change driven by at least two forces.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, the financial and business sector has finally woken up to their responsibility to Earth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yes, I fully expect the governments, to fall short in make the necessary $2.4 trillion annual zero-carbon investments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But at the same time, the global financial asset management sector, with $100 trillion of assets, under the leadership of BlackRock, have starting making substantial progress towards ESG investments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: More than 5,000 corporations have joined the Race to Zero; 1,000 have pledged to Science Based Targets, and I see major private-public partnerships formed to tackle heavy emitting industries, spur new green technologies and drive green procurement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is an emerging consensus that being green is not just the cost of doing business, but also the basic moral standard that consumers expect from businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, there is at least a global consensus that climate justice is important, and the well-off must transfer resources to the less well-off.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Driven by changing consumer expectations and guided by green finance and accounting standards, the private sector can shift towards sustainable production and compensate the affected communities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This can be a huge shift, given that private enterprises, and not governments, are responsible for most production in the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And when there is so much money, so much resources, being directed towards sustainability, towards climate justice, you can imagine that accountability and trust will become absolutely paramount.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But while there are some reasons for being optimistic, there are also hurdles that must be overcome.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, because there are many emerging sustainable finance, accounting and carbon trading standards that are western-centric, there is also an urgent need for them to factor in international, especially Asian perspectives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Another hurdle is that, in this age of stiffening geopolitical competition, there is a risk that sustainability may get weaponised by selected countries or trading blocs to create non-tariff barriers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How can we do this, to capture the possibilities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, actively contribute to the adaption of frameworks and standards for Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Currently, there are many standards and frameworks by key organisations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Just to name a few organizations, they include the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board, Climate Disclosure Standards Board, Global Reporting Initiative, Task Force for Climate Related Climate Disclosure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, there is a lot of work to ensure that what we do here in Asia is compatible and interoperable with the rest of the world, and to ensure that standards are compatible between industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Specifically, this means that Singapore must anchor the Asian chapters of these key international frameworks and standard setting bodies in Singapore to encourage them to work together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We should also actively steer Singapore professional leaders who are in our accounting, auditing and management consulting firms to get involved in these bodies, so that they can build up expertise not just for themselves, but also for younger Singapore-based professionals entering the workforce.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Doing this first task will ensure that the global sustainability framework and standards make sense for Asia and Singapore and that the global standards are of sufficiently high standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, get our sovereign wealth funds, especially Temasek, to spur Singapore companies to embrace and pilot these new green finance and accounting standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While standards for businesses have begun to emerge in London and EU, there is insufficient in-depth corporate adoption.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The adoption efforts of our Temasek-linked companies who are in Asia will go far to ensure that our standards are meaningful and relevant beyond the west.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, through MAS and SGX, push for financial institutes and asset management companies to adhere to these new regulations for both the debt market as well as the equity market.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope that in the process of the Government issuing Government bonds, we can also shape our Government’s approaches in evaluating green investments, so as to shape the Asian norms in green infrastructure financing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must actively anchor emerging ESG fintech, ESG data vendors and depository, and ESG procurement platforms such as G-17 and Matcha Initiative in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also encourage existing companies in Singapore in the credit-rating, asset management space to create ESG solutions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can also get our largest accounting, auditing, management consulting and legal firms to partner with international standards bodies, as well as to establish centres of excellence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Climate Impact X enables the purchases of high-quality carbon credits directly from specific projects, including re-forestation efforts in the region.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When consumers see companies buy high quality carbon credits, their trust in the companies’ action are strengthened, and this sparks a virtuous cycle in spurring companies to do more for the environment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By national utility, I mean that getting our sustainable ecosystem players and our Government agencies to provide cloud-based services, to enable Singapore-based companies to report emissions, purchase green products, and buy carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These areas are very regulatory-driven and are distinct from businesses focused on environment technology or clean energy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the start of my speech, I specifically mentioned creating green collar jobs for mature PMETs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This should not be a surprise to Members in this House given my involvement with the PAP Senior Group.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We all know that ageism exists in certain globally competitive industries, such as international finance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is very hard for mature PMETs to stay in these same industries over the years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They usually then switch over to work for local companies in our domestic sectors, or work in our growing social work or healthcare sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we have a new, emergent area where opportunities are plentiful for our mature PMETs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If they receive the appropriate skills training on sustainable standards, their experience in governance, accounting, finance and cross-border business will be immensely beneficial to the green economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And because this is an emerging area, and one that Singapore can play a role in shaping, I am optimistic that Singapore can shape the industry norm so that ageism does not take root.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To conclude, in my previous speech on climate change, I mentioned that it is difficult for Singapore to achieve net zero emission in the coming decade or two, given the constraints of current technology, given the fact that Singapore serves the world by exporting goods and services, and given that we are resource-poor in terms of renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
