text: But our same status as a manufacturing and services hub of Asia also gives us opportunity to shape the region beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do so by helping them go green.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do so by helping channel resources to the less developed parts of our region in an accountable manner, so that all of us, whether we live in a developed or developing country, can fight climate change together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And at the same time, we must recognise that the greening of the economy is an irreversible tide.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sustainability is now enshrined into the core of what corporate governance is.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If we help our economies and our companies embrace sustainability, we can strengthen our global standing for yet another generation and make Singapore the global-Asia hub of trust, knowledge and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I will like to end by thanking PAP's youth wing, as well as the many climate change activists and passionate business professionals whom I met, for shaping my views in this rapidly changing field.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Motion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I must first declare my interest as Managing Director and Partner of a management consulting firm that does work in climate and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In previous speeches, I have spoken about how climate change, one of the biggest risks facing the world today, can be one of the biggest opportunities for Singapore to lead.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One of these big opportunities is green finance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, Singapore is already ASEAN’s largest green finance market, constituting nearly half of green and sustainability-linked bond and loan issuances.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are ongoing initiatives and partnerships between the Government and industry, such as the Green Finance Industry Taskforce (GFIT) to accelerate green finance in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And there is so much potential to do more.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Green bonds and green loans are now established products.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They need to be scaled up and the known gaps and frictions need to be addressed, as many of my colleagues have discussed today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But to meet the needs of companies and investors in the region and globally, as well as to push for more aggressive, more ambitious targets and hence, higher risk projects, a wider range of products and instruments are needed, including equity, structured products, derivatives, project finance and securities financing in order to provide companies and investors different ways to get financing, invest and manage risk or liquidity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A particularly interesting investment space is climate innovation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Venture capital and private equity investments in climate innovation have grown 14% a year since 2016 to reach $37 billion in 2020, with most funding going into mobility, renewables and waste.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The GFMA report estimates that today, the world is between $90 billion and $210 billion short of the yearly investments in new climate technologies needed to achieve net zero.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a need to bring in high risk and patient capital to fund investments in early stage technologies, start-ups and emerging market firms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The first generation of “green champion” companies – like Enel Group, NextEra Energy, Orsted – they are generating shareholder returns at Big Tech levels, think about the Facebooks and Amazons.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And the second generation, including companies like Beyond Meat and Tesla, are generating returns twice this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But so are the risks, and the time frames for payback long.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, to unlock and catalyse private capital in transition finance and climate innovation, the government and the financial markets should promote the development of blended finance structures, combining public and private capital, in collaboration with national or multilateral development banks, foundations and philanthropic organisations, such as the Gates' Foundation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This must be coupled with Government investment in R&D, including basic research, infrastructure and standards, and smart money from venture capital and private equity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Innovation is critical in green finance – innovation in terms of the the financial products themselves, but also innovation across the green finance ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Just to cite a few examples, leveraging geospatial data for climate risk assessment, AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to facilitate reporting and disclosures, sophisticated scenario analysis and risk modelling, standardisation of legal contract language, as well as tools and platforms for green finance literacy and risk awareness, for corporate boards and executives down to retail investors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These all represent opportunities for Singapore to boost economic growth and create high paying new jobs as we enhance the green finance ecosystem and build green finance capabilities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have built a vibrant financial sector and grown new segments within the sector most recently in fintech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But a key risk to the efficient scaling of the green finance globally is the absence of, or too low carbon pricing and a lack of viable transition pathways for companies to begin.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we are to achieve the objective of making it less expensive for companies to invest in decarbonising and low carbon technologies than to continue emitting carbon, the carbon tax needs to go up, no question.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The question is how we ratchet it up and covering what scope.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Too fast and we risk disadvantaging our companies economically or passing on the cost to end customers; too slow and we risk not achieving our climate KPIs or hurting the companies' own long term resilience and missing the opportunity to create business advantage and value.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each sector has a different emissions profile, transition readiness, industry structure, willingness of the end customer to pay.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I echo the views of the Member, like Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har, that the increase in carbon tax must be phased, I think with the highest emitting sectors first, with explicit forward direction on price levels and ample time for companies to prepare and adjust.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And they must be implemented in a way that is a "just transition", minimising social and economic costs for those least able to bear them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And, in the words of Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, there is already a tectonic shift in capital as asset managers are moving billions and billions of dollars into sustainable strategies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Companies that do not act, may well soon see capital outflows to companies that do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I repeat the call I made in my Budget speech: Singapore should be bold and lead the way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore companies must change their mindset and see climate and the green economy as a big opportunity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Businesses, investors and the Government must invest behind climate innovation and new technologies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And they must build the capabilities, people and skills needed to do this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must all understand the climate risk and opportunity and make informed choices on what we are willing to pay for, if we want to leave a better world for our children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Learn from our youth, many are already making these choices.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Under pre-employment training efforts, also known as PET, may I share the following four points.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, closing current employability gaps of our undergraduates.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over the last decade, our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHL) have also introduced and strengthened curriculum that supports growth in the green sectors though the full-time graduate employment rates in these courses have not been too encouraging.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This lower employment rate of environmental engineers amongst engineering graduates is fairly consistent also in the years 2019 and 2018.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While environmental engineering is not the only sustainability-linked course, it is one of the core offerings.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This posits the need for us to work with the private sector and our IHLs, to better understand the possible causes behind the lagging employment rates of our students in a course directly linked to the green sector.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Whether it is a skills gap, mismatch of skills or a lack of job opportunities for environmental engineers in Singapore, the employability gaps of our current undergraduates need to be studied so that corrective interventions can be made to boost employment rates of our graduates committed to the green sector.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Looking forward, curriculum for up and coming green sectors can be further enhanced in our IHLs with consultation of industry players.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These sectors include environmental logistics, environmental health, architecture and sustainable design, environmental economics amongst others.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some of them are presently offered as electives or post-graduate courses but need to be integrated into the core curriculum of their respective undergraduate schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The greening of jobs also means that sustainability-related topics should be extended to many more course offerings in our IHLs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They come from 115 different departments out of 129, ranging from ecologically conscious art, architecture, film, design and urban planning.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our IHLs can do more to integrate sustainability-focused or related courses across schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After all, the work of stewarding our climate in the present goes beyond conservation, but requires challenging our current attitudes, lifestyles and livelihoods.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: On that note, I would like to suggest for our business schools' adoption, the study of the Economics of Mutuality, also known as EoM.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: EoM is a new business innovation model founded by Bruno Roche, the former Chief Economist of Mars Inc.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This concept advocates that business can deliver superior financial performance precisely because it mobilises and generates human, social and natural capital along with financial capital.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This provides a new lens through which companies look at their business model for a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since 2014, the Oxford University Business School and Rotterdam School of Management have collaborated with Roche separately to set up research and education centres of EoM.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These centres uncover best practices and case studies for businesses and SMEs, and develop teaching curricula.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we transit into a low-carbon economy, a business model of sustainability like the EoM could be taught at both PET and CET levels.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Growing collaborations with industry partners in developing new PET programmes ensure relevance to our markets and workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I look forward to more such industry collaborations supporting green jobs in our PET centres.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Third, complement PET curricula with CET sustainability modules.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As new skills and technology in sustainability are still evolving and being identified, it may be challenging for IHLs to react fast enough to meet the current and evolving needs of companies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: IHLs could consider supplementing curricula with updated modules offered in our CET institutions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This allows our fresh graduates to also be equipped with current and up to date skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These CET modules can continually be updated with industry consultation and be the agile portion of the curricula for our students.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The partnership with the private sector in building green skill sets should extend beyond established firms, to include cutting-edge green startups with new green tech innovations in Europe, UK and the US.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This allows for better understanding of trends, evolving skills and technology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I have three suggestions on how we can support these green tech innovations amongst our fresh graduates.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Green Immersion Programmes, a concept similar to the NUS Overseas College internship programmes, will place our undergraduates with specific firms and countries that excel in the green space.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Sending our students from multi-disciplinary backgrounds to be immersed in cultures supporting entrepreneurial spirit in green spaces, will not only support the growth of green startups, but also the greening of our jobs in various sectors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Industry players may include MNCs who are exploring new product offerings or new startups.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With the concentration of academia in research and real-time input from industry on challenges faced, as well as funding from private investors, iCAST serves as a perfect incubator for accelerated growth in sustainable technologies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: An expanded Singapore version of such a centre, which I will coin as Centre of Innovation for Green Technologies for now, could be formed in partnership with other nations with advanced green technology, with Singapore’s value-add in contextualising application of GreenTech with and for our regional counterparts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We can imagine that Singapore could one day set up an Institute of Sustainability Leadership for Asia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This institute will house the above Centre of Innovation for Green Technologies, the Singapore Green Finance Centre and other green centres for logistics, buildings and corporate governance in Asia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Suggestion three: complement private-sector efforts in supporting green innovations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is extremely heartening to see how the private sector had stepped in to support green innovations in recent years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Government could perhaps find ways to complement such private sector initiatives through providing business infrastructure support for winning firms, while also exploring traineeship programmes for our workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is a win-win for the firms and our people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Moving to CET, also known as Continuing Education and Training efforts, amongst the non-traditional green sectors in Singapore, we see finance, transport and building sectors hiring sustainability-related positions, with the rest catching up.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The greening of sectors will take place only as each gainfully considers incorporating sustainability concepts in their processes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In order to create green jobs, there must first be a demand and a market value for such work, and ultimately, for companies, especially for our SMEs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In overseas markets with high green consciousness, consumers proactively look to support firms that have a green agenda when they make purchases or investment decisions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This becomes a strong motivator for companies to include green competencies in their job pool and hence, generate green jobs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Greater engagement with our community groups, grassroots and schools to uncover and overcome obstacles in mindset change, will work well to complement the ongoing good work of Government agencies like NEA.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We all have a responsibility to current and future generations to do our best to mitigate the negative impacts of climate change, while there is still hope.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This means our transition to a low-carbon society must benefit not just Singapore, but Singaporeans as a whole.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To me, this also means our strategy cannot be "go green" at any and all costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is why the Singapore Green Plan 2030, launched in February last year, is a comprehensive strategy, which includes a green economy as one of its five key pillars.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I aim to speak quickly on the green economy in three areas: transitioning to a world with carbon tax, carbon trading and green financing employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This year's review of the carbon tax level and its forward trajectory will be an opportune time to further elaborate on plans for our carbon taxation system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In doing so, perhaps, the Government can consider the following few points.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of reviewing our carbon tax rate every three to four years, can we establish a fixed formula for the carbon tax rate to evolve over a longer period of time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like a similar mechanism introduced in the EU, this aims to prevent carbon leakage, that is, companies transferring production to countries where climate change measures are looser than in Singapore and are "cheaper" to comply with.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, this measure can help to promote greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction efforts in countries outside Singapore and to spur others to take climate change measures seriously.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Three, as we increase carbon taxes and if we do so in various ways and various levels, I ask for carbon pricing to be part of a comprehensive mitigation strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It should contain support measures to enhance the effectiveness and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Member, Mr Dennis Tan mentioned about just transition measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I would like to add on that just transition measures are indeed needed to assist low-income households and vulnerable workers when it is introduced.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One possibility is to first set the carbon tax level at least around US$8 to US$9 tCO2e, using S&P Platts CEC as a spot reference, or slightly higher to inject some urgency for emitters to accelerate their decarbonising plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That floor is where the voluntary market is valuing and trading carbon "credits", a concept that I will turn to now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The other main way countries use to bring down carbon emissions is to establish a cap-and-trade system which caps the total level of greenhouse gas emissions and allow companies with low emissions to sell their extra carbon "credits" or "offsets" to larger emitters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also the voluntary carbon markets for companies and individuals, which can co-exist with compliance markets created and driven by regulation, essentially for companies or individuals to buy carbon credits voluntarily to offset their unavoidable emissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Carbon markets allow for companies to buy and sell these tradable carbon credits that represent reduction, avoidance or removal of a certain amount of emissions from the atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Depending on different price scenarios and their underlying drivers, the market size in 2030 could be between $5 billion and $30 billion at the low end and more than $50 billion at the high end.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The race to decarbonise in Asia is picking up pace with China introducing its national carbon market in third quarter last year, while other ASEAN nations, including Malaysia, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand and Philippines, have taken steps towards establishing their own frameworks to trade carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore has also pledged to reduce carbon emission intensity by 36% from 2005 levels by 2030.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is therefore unsurprising that Singapore already plans to become a carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is among the various recommendations of the Future Economy Council's Emerging Strong Taskforce (EST) in May 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to do this fast as part of our green growth plans as other countries in the region are also looking into it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite the opportunities, the carbon trading market has long been plagued by low liquidity, poor risk-management, limited data availability and inadequate financing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the establishment of Climate Impact X, a new global carbon exchange established in Singapore to facilitate the sale of large-scale, high-quality carbon credits, is undoubtedly a promising development, it will be useful if the Government can share on how the carbon trading value chain is progressing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would also be good to know our plans to further tap on Singapore's reputation for integrity and strength in professional and financial services, such as to establish a carbon credit registry to serve Asia, much like the Verra Registry and the Gold Standard Impact Registry in the US.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a need to build or enhance the ecosystem which needs to link up the four types of key players: the upstream project developers, NGOs that certify the projects, brokers and traders to facilitate the access to carbon credits and end users, such as companies or individuals committing to offset part or all of their GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another aspect is we can also enhance the existing exchanges here as it develops standardised contracts for carbon credits and set a benchmark price.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, from an infrastructure perspective, the Government can and must eventually work on the regulatory oversight of carbon markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would enhance the integrity and standards of carbon credits traded here, making us more attractive as a hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, there may be a need to have plans to roll our developmental courses that we can upskill Singaporeans to take advantage of these new economic trends, especially those in the banking and financial services sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Finally, on the prospects for green financing employment growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our economy shifts towards a greener one, new employment opportunities in the green economy will emerge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The "Skills Demand for the Future Economy” Report released last year by SkillsFuture Singapore identified the green economy as a key job growth area for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can expect more jobs to be greener.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are now almost half a million jobs in low-carbon businesses and their supply chains across the UK.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of which, it was estimated that there were about 6,500 employment in the sub-sectors of low carbon financial and advisory services (as of 2018).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, we need to find ways to develop a pool of talent to help Singapore remain as an attractive destination for businesses, especially those who place a premium on sustainability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important for the Government and businesses to help workers to equip themselves to take on these green jobs – whether within existing sectors or in new sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Time and opportunity cost on the part of the workers must also be factored in to allow them to acquire the new skills and to adapt to a greener business environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One sector is the financial sector which will play an important role to provide the investment for sustainability projects and in turn, help to shape a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must build and maintain the pipeline of green workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the green financing sector grows, we will need to groom human capital early with the know-how to align investments with sustainability and green finance principles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is hoped, therefore, that more people will attend these workshops.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that the Government will do more.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, but beyond all these domestic efforts, our greening of the financial sector allows for a more effective way for Singapore to engage regional partners to accelerate regional climate sustainability projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what more can be done to engage and work with regional partners to accelerate regional climate sustainability which will be more effective in the long run?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a fine balance to ensure that we achieve an "inclusive transition" to a low-carbon economy, with the participation of companies, financial institutions and other stakeholders in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In doing so, we must train to capitalise on new opportunities, strike the right balance to manage the trade-offs, and do more to raise awareness of our efforts to build a green economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sustainable development requires the committed pursuit of a triple "P" bottom line of profit, people, and the planet.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This framework advances the goal of sustainability in business practices, in which enterprises look beyond profits and incorporate social and environmental issues to measure their overall business performance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To achieve a triple "P" bottom line, enterprises re-direct profits towards green technology and reskilling of workers for the green economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A green economy does not necessarily equate to higher business costs and unemployment rates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the right strategies and good execution, businesses can reduce costs, improve productivity rates and ensure that more workers enjoy purposeful employment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More importantly, this leads to a net positive outcome for our planet.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As seen in many parts of the world, carbon tax regimes have been put in place to send an economic signal to move people towards a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because a levy of a tax without actual transformation would simply lead to a pass through of cost and eventually lead to a rise in cost of living.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could deepen societal fault lines between those who have the resources to go green and those who do not.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must not allow the transition towards a greener economy to be a source of division in our society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe an example of an industry that is poised to achieve a triple "P" bottom line is the built industry.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Current Building Management Software (BMS) can analyse for actionable insights to ensure that energy usage commensurate with the level of occupancy and activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: BMS can also proactively support predictive maintenance which improves plant resiliency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The adoption of BMS presents an opportunity for enterprises to align themselves to the triple "P" bottom line.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: BMS lowers energy consumption, thereby helping businesses reduce energy related costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These cost savings would be further welcomed given our current elevated energy price levels.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Preventive maintenance reduces downtimes caused by faulty equipment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Predictive maintenance reduces over-maintenance of equipment that are in good conditions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reduces time and trips leading to an increase in labour productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The combined reduction of energy consumption, longer equipment lifespan caused by preventive maintenance and optimisation of trips reduces carbon footprint and move our enterprises towards all triple P bottom lines.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To support the transformation of industries like that of smart building management, there is a need to aid companies in upskilling their employees so that they are empowered to achieve a sustainable green outcome.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, upskilling programmes cannot be pursued in silo.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They need to be integrated in two broad ways.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digital solutions are necessary to monitor, track and report various parameters.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond reporting, industries will need to know how to leverage the data and translate into tangible actions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is starting from a good base as we have invested heavily in empowering our workforce and industries to be digitally ready.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government can scale up programmes that tap on the vast range of skillsets possessed by our private sector partners.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government should continue to seek out pathfinders and interlocutors to ensure job opportunities for our workers and a ready pool of businesses who can embark on green transformation programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, I had the opportunity to speak with Johnson Controls, who is a global provider in smart building management solutions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Johnson Controls partnered SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and Ngee Ann Polytechnic in rolling out a SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides equipping participants with domain knowledge such as building services management and green building management, the course also imparts foundational digital skills.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Learning is further enriched by on-job training within various departments at Johnson Controls.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Adopting an integrated approach towards upskilling programmes will ensure better alignment between new skills, new purposeful jobs and the expertise industries need to go green.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The crucial challenge before us is to provide industries and Singaporean workers the tools, resources and skills to capitalise on the confluence of these various elements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enforcing a carbon tax regime is not a silver bullet that can guarantee our transition to a greener economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Climate change is an urgent global concern and would require collective and coordinated global action to address, as the scale of effort needed to make a meaningful impact far exceeds what individual countries can achieve.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a small island state, we are particularly susceptible to even small changes in global temperature, which will affect anything from sea level to weather patterns to food production and even supply of fresh water.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, our journey towards sustainability started decades ago.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Given our limited natural resources and the lack of a hinterland, we have been pushing the envelope to conserve and maximise critical resources such as land and water, and green our island even as we embark on industrialisation and urbanisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, as we make the transition towards a greener future, we will need to make trade-offs and accept changes to the way we live and work.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, as businesses introduce greener methods of production, production costs may go up because of the use of greener materials or greener ways of disposing waste.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some may require significant investments in new and greener equipment or need technologies that are yet to be available.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This may eventually translate to higher costs for consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But as Prof Koh Lian Pin pointed out, we will be doing ourselves a disservice if we focus only on the higher costs in the short-to-medium term and lose sight of the larger and longer-term opportunities that sustainability movement brings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must continue to act decisively to prepare ourselves for these opportunities, while pacing our transition in a calibrated manner and managing the trade-offs and cost impact carefully, as Ms Poh Li San, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Derrick Goh pointed out.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister Grace Fu will speak about Singapore's planning ahead and acting decisively on green transition, including the ambitious steps that we are taking.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will elaborate on what we intend to do on the economic front.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are a number of exciting economic opportunities arising from the global movement towards sustainability that play to Singapore's strengths as a transport, advanced manufacturing, trading and financial hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Several Members, including Mr Don Wee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Henry Kwek, as well as Ms Mariam Jafaar and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned green financing; and Mr Saktiandi Supaat too.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As countries step up their efforts towards their climate change commitments, there will be growing demand for green financing, as well as investments into green technologies, infrastructure and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore has established itself as a trusted financial and business hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are well placed to capture emerging opportunities in green financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, we are already a market leader in Southeast Asia for sustainable debt.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The sector is still evolving and there is great potential as demand for green finance continues to grow in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Don Wee also asked the Government to consider issuing more green bonds.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Yes, we are exploring opportunities to do so under MOF's Green Bonds Programme Office.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Carbon services and carbon credits will play an increasingly important role to help businesses and governments meet regulatory or voluntary climate goals.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Prof Koh Lian Pin, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, we can build on Singapore's foundation as a trusted and deep commodities trading hub as well as the vast potential for the creation of nature-based credits in our region to become a carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also working with like-minded partners to standardise the rules on cross-border transactions of credits and to build the infrastructure and processes to facilitate this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, arising from the efforts of the Singapore Emerging Stronger Taskforce's Alliance for Action on Sustainability, DBS, SGX, Standard Chartered and Temasek have set up the Climate Impact Exchange or CIX.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: CIX provides a carbon exchange and marketplace for companies to access high quality carbon credits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This exchange will have high standards of disclosure and emphasis on high quality carbon credits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is how we can differentiate ourselves and avoid greenwashing problems mentioned by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over a longer timeframe, there are also opportunities in low-carbon technologies such as hydrogen, sustainable aviation and maritime fuels, smart electricity grids and sustainable foods.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are investing research and development resources into these areas which we would need for ourselves and we hope to build new economic engines in the process.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These new green activities are exciting, but they will take time to grow and mature.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, most of our existing enterprises will be affected by the green wave.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is because investors, lenders, customers and regulatory agencies will increasingly impose environmental requirements on these enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The impact will differ for different sectors and enterprises, depending on the nature of their businesses and operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The impact is most significant for the largest emitting sectors such as the petrochemical industry.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have been working with businesses in the sector to help them decarboniese.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Last November, we released the Sustainable Jurong Island report, which outlines our plan to transform Jurong Island into a sustainable energy and chemicals park that operates sustainably and exports sustainable products globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The journey is a challenging one but we are determined to get there.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our power sector, which provides electricity for both businesses and households is also a major emitter.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, EMA has schemes to facilitate the sale of excess electricity to the grid and we will continue to help and support them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also develop and tap on low-carbon solutions, such as hydrogen and carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS), when these become more viable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, we will work with generation companies to enhance the efficiency of our power generation systems.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But lower emitting businesses will also need to incorporate sustainability as an integral part of their business and embrace sustainability as a competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, more tourists and international conferences now require that countries and hotels they are visiting to have met certain sustainability standards.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am encouraged that a recent survey by the Sustainable Living Lab with Singapore Business Federation and other partners found that our SMEs recognise additional market opportunities, reputation improvements and cost reductions as the top three motivations for them to consider becoming more sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will explain later how we can provide a conducive environment to help our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our third aim is to equip our workers with relevant skills so that they can benefit from the green economy, as Ms Hany Soh, Ms Rachel Ong, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Edward Chia highlighted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the green economy develops, many green jobs will be created that will require new green skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, a traditional car mechanic will need now to learn how to repair an electric vehicle.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: An internal combustion engine is very different from an electric motor.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A power engineer will now need to learn about hydrogen, solar and other renewable forms of energies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: An investment manager will need to learn about sustainability standards and green financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: SkillsFuture Singapore identified the green economy as a growth area in their inaugural report on skills demand for the future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are green job opportunities in many sectors, such as financial services, energy and power, built environment and manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are also skills that are transferable across sectors, such as carbon footprint management and sustainability management.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These skills can equip our existing workforce to take on new jobs or new roles in existing jobs in the new green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Workforce Singapore (WSG) is working with partners to explore a broad-based career conversion programme (CCP) for sustainability professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This CCP will not only help companies nurture "sustainability champions" to kickstart their journey, but also support the transition of affected workers due to the greening of their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the sectoral level, efforts are underway to build our talent pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: WSG and Singapore Polytechnic have rolled out a new CCP for clean and renewable energy professionals in September 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Separately, MAS is setting up centres of excellence for training and research in green financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have three such centres in Singapore – the Singapore Green Finance Centre by SMU and Imperial College Business School, the Sustainable and Green Finance Institute established by NUS and the Sustainable Finance Institute Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: MAS will also be launching a new Sustainable Finance Technical Skills and Competency category in the Skills Framework for Financial Services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These efforts support our workers in building the relevant knowledge and skills which can, in turn, help anchor Singapore as a leading centre for green finance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To achieve these ambitions, I agree with many Members that the Government needs to work in partnership with the private sector and the community.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government's role is to provide an enabling environment to help businesses and workers take advantage of these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, we will need to right-price resources through the carbon tax, which Minister Grace Fu will speak on later and which Mr Louis Ng also mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The correct pricing will guide investment decisions and spur companies to decarbonise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But it will also come with higher costs for businesses and consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We should calibrate and pace the adjustment carefully to give companies sufficient time to adapt, put in place decarbonisation measures and stay competitive, as Members, including Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Derrick Goh, mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A higher carbon tax will also have an indirect impact on households.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will consider how we can help ease the cost increase, especially for the lower-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For instance, when the carbon tax was first introduced in 2019, the Government provided additional U-Save rebates for three years to cover the expected average increase in electricity and gas bills from the carbon tax.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also subsequently introduced the Climate Friendly Households Programme to provide eligible households with vouchers to offset the cost of energy-efficient appliances.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, we will complement the carbon tax with financial support to help companies adapt.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will support training workshops, capability and product development projects and key enablers, such as certification and financing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Several of these efforts will involve partnerships with the trade associations and chambers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also leverage the green finance drive to provide another incentive for companies to become more sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Green and Sustainability Loan Grant Scheme (GSLS) that MAS rolled out in November 2020 encourages banks to develop green and sustainability-linked loan frameworks to make such financing more accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises to better support their transition to greener business models.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The GSLS helps defray qualifying expenses incurred by businesses and banks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, we are developing standards and accreditation to help companies assess and demonstrate their sustainability credentials.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To date, the Singapore Standards Council and the Singapore Accreditation Council have developed more than 50 national standards and 13 accreditation programmes supporting the green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Examples include standards in renewable energy, electric vehicles and food sustainability and resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We developed these standards in consultation with industry associations, professional bodies, Institutes of Higher Learning, research institutes and companies to ensure they are relevant and robust.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore is also an active member of the two international standards setting bodies, the ISO as well as the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), at the technical and governance levels.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, Singapore is involved in the development of new ISO and IEC standards in the areas of water efficiency management, waste terminology, solar, photovoltaic and circular economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the governance level, Singapore also chairs the ISO technical management board that oversees some 300 technical committees, including in sustainability, such as for sustainable finance, circular economy and environmental management.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Fourth, we are helping our companies access green opportunities abroad through the Green Economy Agreements (GEA).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, the GEA would set common rules and standards that would promote trade and investment in environmental goods and services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, the GEA would facilitate cooperation in areas, such as the scaling of low-carbon technology and pilot projects.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: GEAs will build on and enhance Singapore's economic connectivity established through our extensive network of trade agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They will also strengthen international governance on trade and environmental sustainability and put us in good stead to contribute to international discourse on rules writing and standards setting in the global response to climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will help us build knowledge and develop capabilities and place us in a stronger position to capture green opportunities in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are challenges for our businesses in transiting to a more sustainable business model.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are also immense opportunities for our enterprises and workers in the rapidly growing green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will help foster the right environment for businesses and workers to adapt to and take advantage of these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms He Ting Ru mentioned, every one of us has a role to play to support the sustainability movement, do our part to conserve resources, minimise waste and opt for greener products and services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On this note, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I would also like to thank Members, Ms Poh Li San, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Don Wee for sponsoring today’s Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This Motion draws attention to the importance of developing Singapore’s green economy and ensuring an inclusive transition towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: On behalf of my colleagues at MSE and across the Government, allow me to express our deep appreciation for the many good and fresh perspectives and constructive suggestions that Members have put forth, including those submitted by the Young PAP.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A year ago, this House passed a Motion declaring climate change a global emergency and a threat to mankind.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The latest science has given even stronger evidence on the urgency for action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report published last August, human influence has unequivocally warmed the climate.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Without strong and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, global temperature rise will exceed 2°C within this century, increasing the intensity and propensity of extreme weather events, such as floods, droughts and wildfires and accelerating biodiversity loss in every part of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Some of these harsh realities are already being felt today, as seen by recent record-breaking floods in Southeast Asia, prolonged drought in South America, high temperatures and raging wildfires in North America, followed by extraordinary snowfall.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As a small, low-lying island in the tropics, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to sea level rise.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Climate change is an existential threat to us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One year on, our efforts to accelerate climate action and embrace sustainable development have grown stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched last February, agencies have made considerable headway.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the coming weeks, the five leading Ministries for the Green Plan will deliver updates on the progress of key initiatives and share their outlook and focus areas for the year ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A similar "green awakening" is rapidly spreading across the globe.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the start of 2020, there were only 18 countries with net zero aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, the number has grown to 84, including the world’s five largest emitters, accounting for almost 90% of global emissions and over 90% of global GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Despite the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, countries have sought to incorporate sustainability and climate action in their recovery plans, laying groundwork for the transition to a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last November, I had the privilege of leading the Singapore delegation at the 26th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26).

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As the first conference of such a scale and scope since the pandemic, COP26 was a landmark opportunity to rally the world around the climate action clarion call.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: World leaders, businesses and civil society organisations came out in full force, emphasising the need to raise our collective mitigation ambition significantly in this critical decade.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: COP26 had laid a firm foundation and accelerated the momentum for global climate action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A substantive and balanced package of decisions, known as the Glasgow Climate Pact, was forged through hard-earned consensus and compromise.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Pact will scale up climate action and drive capability- and capacity-building efforts to keep a 1.5-degree climate change within reach.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore will do our part to meet our international obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will review our policies and actions under the Green Plan, while managing our inherent constraints and trade-offs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will also expand our options for reducing emissions through international partnerships and in step with global advancements in low-carbon technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will review our targets and raise our climate ambition, and as Prof Koh Lian Pin highlighted, ensure that our targets are backed by the right strategies, policies and actions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As a responsible member of the international community, Singapore has been working hard to support a multilateral rules-based approach to address climate change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Article 6, which governs market and non-market cooperative mechanisms towards emission reduction, was the sole outstanding issue under the Paris Agreement Work Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For countries with limited domestic abatement potential such as Singapore, these mechanisms will present new pathways to raise ambition, as Ms Poh Li San mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At COP26, we also supported various global partnerships and initiatives aimed at raising global climate action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We endorsed the Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use to affirm our collective commitment to sustainable land use.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We joined various other voluntary coalitions, pledging to reduce global methane emissions, green government operations and cultivate climate-smart agriculture.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our membership in these coalitions will facilitate the sharing of best practices and collaboration with like-minded countries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore will continue playing a constructive role to sustain the momentum for global climate action and support fellow small states and developing countries to build capacity and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Corporates are playing a critical role in driving the global transition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are increasingly focused on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) issues, striving to do well and do good at the same time.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With greater demand from investors, activists and consumers, more businesses are paying attention to their triple bottom lines of Profit, People and the Planet, as Mr Edward Chia noted.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Among them are Singapore companies such as City Developments Limited (CDL), Olam International, Singtel and the Singapore Exchange (SGX).

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Greater private sector involvement will be a multiplier, bolstering our collective response.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Civil society and community organisations also play an instrumental role.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As advocates, they raise awareness on the importance of climate action, and organise ground-up initiatives to rally the community for climate action and environmental sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At COP26, I was glad to meet Singaporean representatives from a diverse range of backgrounds: academia, youth groups, businesses, NGOs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Like Mr Louis Ng, I was inspired by their passion and aspirations for a greener Singapore and the various projects and platforms they have mounted to make a difference.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Esther, Cheryl, Swati, Xiang Tian, Wei Shan – these are all representatives of how much energy we have found in our corporate as well as our NGO people sector.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Hany Soh said many residents also take pride in championing sustainability initiatives through the Action for Green Towns initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Going green is no longer an option, but a strategic transition we must undertake to thrive in a carbon- and resource-constrained future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The transition will have far-ranging implications on every facet of society, including our lifestyle and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This Motion is therefore timely, as we are building the necessary foundations for Singapore’s transition to a low-carbon society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government has every intent, as this Motion states, to partner the private sector, civil society and the community in turning our collective goals in the Green Plan into reality.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If we work together and make the right choices, the low-carbon transition can yield significant opportunities and rewards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is in Singapore’s interest to secure an early foothold in emerging growth areas so as to reap valuable dividends and future-proof our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa mentioned, the latent economic opportunities in Southeast Asia are immense, if the region maximises its potential to export innovative products and expands its green service offerings.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Miss Rachel Ong also described vivid examples of innovation opportunities created by the global sustainability wave, which our youths and workers can participate in.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As with all transitions, there will invariably be disruptions and trade-offs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry Mr Gan Kim Yong and several Members spoke about some of the structural challenges for large emitters in the hard-to-abate sectors, such as the petrochemical and electricity generation industries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Some businesses and households may have to brace themselves for temporary cost increases.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Transition costs can also manifest in intangible ways, such as the inconvenience from changing our habits and the way we live, work and play.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Yet we must press on, for inaction will cost us even more dearly.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Without prompt and effective mitigation, the detrimental effects of climate change will be exacerbated.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While the direct impacts may be clear, the indirect costs, while less immediately apparent, can be even more significant, as Prof Euston Quah and Tan Jun Rui have argued in a recent Straits Times article.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, floods can claim lives and damage infrastructure, but also displace local communities, raise food prices and disrupt critical supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With the accelerated global shift towards a low-carbon future, businesses which do not adjust face the risk of shrinking demand, stranded assets and becoming obsolete.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is, therefore, in the best interests of businesses, the economy and the nation at large to make this crucial transition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Deputy Speaker, the transition to a low-carbon society will not be straightforward or a quick fix.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To engender an effective and inclusive transition, we have our work cut out.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Gan has spoken about the concrete steps we are taking to capture green growth opportunities, transform businesses and industries, and equip our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Allow me to elaborate on a few other key areas raised by Members.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, raising carbon pricing; second, leveraging carbon markets; and third, strengthening corporate accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I note that Members from both sides of the aisle have spoken in support of the need for a carbon tax and for a higher carbon tax, either at this debate or at the debate last year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am not sure if this assumption is correct; I tried to listen very carefully, I have not heard anyone asking to remove a carbon tax or asking for it to be lowered.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, I take it the assumption that the rationale for a carbon tax is supported by Members of the House on both sides of the aisle, and also the call for a higher carbon tax is an equally shared view by both sides of the House.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, if this assumption is wrong, please correct me.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have heard a wide spectrum of views and proposals on this matter.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members such as Mr Louis Ng have spoken on the need for an appropriate carbon pricing policy that drives emissions reduction effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While others such as Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har argued for the need to preserve our competitiveness, to pace our increases, given the weakness of a post-COVID-19 recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This speaks to the complex and difficult considerations that influence our approach to carbon pricing.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The carbon tax is central to our climate mitigation strategy and complements our suite of abatement efforts across all sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By pricing the cost of CO2 emissions, the carbon tax enhances the business case to implement energy efficiency improvements and other emission reduction solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These shifts in decisions are vital to ensuring the long-term viability of business investments and activities in a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Indeed, we observe that carbon-tax liable companies have accelerated the implementation of decarbonisation projects.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The impact of a carbon price goes beyond current industries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It also ensures that Singapore attracts the right kinds of future investments that are aligned with our low-carbon vision.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over time, a stronger price signal is needed to steer our economy towards a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will tilt the scales further in favour of more innovative low-carbon technologies, driving companies to take bolder steps towards decarbonisation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will also keep Singapore’s carbon tax trajectory in line with the broader international momentum on climate action and support the review of our climate targets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As many Members have noted, the carbon tax should provide a broad-based pricing signal across the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: That is indeed the approach we have taken, as Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean had explained at last year's Motion on Climate Change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This coverage is one of the highest in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But we must also balance the need to extend coverage against the potential administrative costs on businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hence, we have taken the practical approach of setting the existing carbon tax threshold at 25,000 tonnes, which ensures that the carbon tax is applied at key nodes and then flows through to the rest of the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This reduces the administrative load on small emitters, especially SMEs, to measure, report and verify their emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will, however, continue to encourage small emitters to track their carbon footprint on a voluntary basis and indeed, a growing number has begun to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We agree with Mr Derrick Goh and Ms Foo Mee Har on the need to support companies along their decarbonisation journey with revenue from the carbon tax.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Some of the carbon tax revenue is also used to manage the impact of the carbon tax on households.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plan, we have channelled additional funds towards the research, development and demonstration of low-carbon technologies, such as hydrogen and carbon capture utilisation and storage though initiatives such as the Low-Carbon Energy Research Funding Initiative (LCER FI).

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More broadly, we have also increased investments in the urban solutions and sustainability research domain to help us better understand the impact of climate change on Singapore and develop novel solutions for sustainability, such as protecting our coastline, finding cheaper ways of reducing emissions and keeping our homes and offices cool.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And this is one point that Ms Mariam Jaafar has raised, about patient capital and investments in the long run, and the Government has been investing significantly in new technologies in the sustainability arena.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over the past months, the Government has consulted businesses and engaged the public on the need for and the potential impact of a higher carbon tax, as part of our review of the post-2023 carbon tax level and trajectory.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
